questions.question: You indicated in the survey that you like to travel within your country. Tell me about a place in your country that you enjoy visiting. Where is it, and what is it like there?

il.text: I like to visit Busan. It is a big city by the sea. There are many beaches. The seafood is very fresh and delicious. I go there by train. I visit Busan every summer.
My favorite place is Jeju Island. It is very beautiful. There are many beaches and a big mountain. The weather is warm. I like to drive around the island. I want to go again soon.

im1.text: I really like to visit Gangneung. It is a city on the east coast of Korea. It takes about two hours from Seoul by train. Gangneung has beautiful beaches with clear water. There is also a famous coffee street near the beach, so I always drink coffee and look at the ocean. The seafood is also very good there. I like Gangneung because it is relaxing.

My favorite place to visit in Korea is Jeonju. It is famous for its traditional Korean houses, called hanok. There is a big hanok village, and many people wear traditional clothes and take pictures there. Jeonju is also famous for bibimbap, and the food is really delicious. The city is not very big, so I can walk everywhere. I visit Jeonju once a year with my friends.

im2.text: One place I love to visit in Korea is Jeju Island. It's an island in the south, and it takes about an hour by plane from Seoul. Jeju is famous for its beautiful nature. There's a big mountain called Hallasan in the middle of the island, and there are many beaches with clear blue water. The island also has unique stone walls and lots of tangerine farms. When I go there, I usually rent a car and drive along the coast. The scenery is amazing, especially at sunset. I also like eating black pork barbecue, which is a famous local food. I think Jeju is the best place in Korea to relax.

I really enjoy visiting Gyeongju. It's a city in the southeast of Korea, and it was the capital of an old kingdom called Silla. Because of that, the city has a lot of history. There are old temples, like Bulguksa, and many royal tombs that look like small green hills. At night, some of the historic places are lit up, so they look really beautiful. The city is quiet and not very crowded compared to Seoul. I usually rent a bike and ride around the old town. Whenever I visit Gyeongju, I feel like I'm traveling back in time.
phrases: I feel like I'm traveling back in time

im3.text: The place I enjoy visiting the most in Korea is Busan. It's the second largest city in the country, and it's on the southeast coast, so it's a nice mix of city life and the ocean. It takes about two and a half hours from Seoul by high-speed train. The most famous spot is Haeundae Beach, which gets really crowded in summer. Personally, though, I prefer the quieter beaches and the small villages on the hills, where the houses are painted in bright colors. Another thing I love is the food. There's a big fish market by the port, and you can choose fresh seafood and eat it right there. Every time I go to Busan, I feel more energetic, maybe because of the sea breeze.

I'd like to tell you about Sokcho, a small city on the east coast. It's one of my favorite places because it has both the mountains and the sea. On one side of the city, there's Seoraksan, a famous mountain with amazing rocky peaks, and on the other side, there's a long, sandy beach. In the fall, the leaves on the mountain turn red and yellow, and a lot of people come to hike. The city also has a big seafood market where you can try local dishes. I usually stay at a small guesthouse near the beach and wake up early to watch the sunrise over the ocean. It's quiet and peaceful there, which is exactly what I need after a busy week.
phrases: both the mountains and the sea
On one side of the city
which is exactly what I need

ih.text: If I had to pick one place in Korea that I never get tired of, it would definitely be Jeju Island. It's a volcanic island off the southern coast, and you can get there in about an hour by plane from Seoul. What makes Jeju special is how different it feels from the mainland. The island is covered with black volcanic rocks, and people use them to build low stone walls around their fields. Right in the middle of the island stands Hallasan, the highest mountain in South Korea. Along the coast, there are beaches with turquoise water, little cafés with ocean views, and walking trails that go all the way around the island. I usually rent a car and drive along the coastal road with no real plan. Jeju always gives me a sense of freedom that I can't get in the city.
phrases: If I had to pick one place

ih.text: One place I really enjoy is Jeonju, a city in the southwestern part of Korea. It's best known for its hanok village, which is a large area full of traditional Korean houses with curved tile roofs. Walking through the narrow alleys there feels like stepping into a historical drama. Many visitors rent traditional clothes called hanbok and take photos in front of the old buildings, and honestly, I've done that too. Jeonju is also famous for its food. Bibimbap is the most famous dish, but there are also lots of street food stalls selling things like grilled skewers and sweet snacks. In the evening, the village gets quieter, and the lanterns along the streets make everything look warm and cozy. I think what I like most is that it's a place where old and new Korea exist side by side.

al.text: The place in Korea I find myself going back to again and again is Gyeongju, an old city in the southeast. For almost a thousand years, it was the capital of the Silla kingdom, so the whole city is basically an open-air museum. What surprised me the first time I visited was that there are huge royal tombs right in the middle of town. They look like gentle green hills, and you'll see people walking their dogs or having picnics right next to them. Then there's Bulguksa, a beautiful temple on the side of a mountain, and nearby there's a famous stone Buddha inside a small cave. At night, the old palace pond is lit up, and the reflection of the buildings on the water is honestly one of the most beautiful things I've ever seen in Korea. Besides the history, I love that the historic areas don't have tall apartment blocks everywhere. It feels calm and spacious, and it reminds me to slow down. Every time I visit, I discover something I missed before.
phrases: I find myself going back to
it reminds me to slow down

al.text: If you asked me where in Korea I'd go for a perfect weekend, I'd say Gangneung without even thinking. It's a coastal city on the east side of the country, and since the high-speed train line opened, you can get there from Seoul in about two hours, which makes it ideal for a short getaway. The beaches there are wide and clean, and the water is a deep, almost unreal shade of blue. What really sets Gangneung apart, though, is its coffee culture. There's a whole street lined with cafés facing the ocean, and you can spend an entire afternoon just sipping coffee and watching the waves. The city also has a quieter, more traditional side. There's a lovely lake with a walking path around it and a historic house where a famous scholar was born. And of course, you can't leave without trying the local tofu dishes, which are made with seawater. I usually have a bowl for breakfast before heading to the beach. It's the kind of place where you arrive tired and leave completely recharged.

questions.tip_ko: 도시 이름과 위치, 가는 방법을 먼저 말하고 볼거리·먹거리를 하나씩 붙여요. 확실히 아는 사실만 골라 말해도 충분해요.

questions.question: When you plan a trip somewhere in your country, how do you usually get ready? Tell me about the things you do before you leave and on the day of the trip.

il.text: Before a trip, I find a hotel on the internet. Then I buy train tickets. I pack my bag the night before. I bring clothes and a phone charger. On the day of the trip, I wake up early.
I plan my trip with my friends. We choose a place together. Then we book a hotel. I make a list of good restaurants. On the day of the trip, we meet at the station in the morning.

im1.text: When I plan a trip in Korea, I start about two weeks before. First, I choose the place and check the weather. Then I book a hotel and buy bus or train tickets online. I also look for famous restaurants and places to visit on the internet. The night before the trip, I pack my bag with clothes, a charger, and some snacks. On the day of the trip, I leave home early.
phrases: I start about two weeks before

im1.text: My family usually travels by car, so I help my parents get ready. A few days before the trip, we decide where to go and book a place to stay. My mom prepares snacks and drinks for the car. My dad checks the car. On the morning of the trip, we leave very early to avoid traffic. I usually listen to music and sleep in the car.
phrases: A few days before the trip

im2.text: Well, I'm a pretty organized person, so I prepare a lot before a trip. About a month before, I decide where to go and look at travel blogs to get ideas. Then I book my train tickets and a hotel, because they get expensive if I wait too long. A week before the trip, I make a simple schedule with the places I want to see and the restaurants I want to try. The night before, I pack my bag and check the weather again. On the day of the trip, I always leave early and buy a coffee at the station. I really enjoy this planning process.

To be honest, I don't plan much for trips in Korea. Usually, my friends and I decide where to go just a few days before. One of us books a guesthouse, and another person checks the bus or train times. I don't make a detailed schedule because I like to be spontaneous. The night before, I just pack some comfortable clothes, my phone charger, and a portable battery. On the day of the trip, we meet at the bus terminal and buy snacks for the ride. When we arrive, we ask local people or search online for good places to eat.

im3.text: Whenever I plan a trip within Korea, I follow pretty much the same steps. First, I pick a destination based on the season. For example, I go to the beach in summer and to the mountains in the fall. Then I check train tickets right away, because popular routes sell out quickly on weekends. After that, I look for a place to stay, and I usually choose a small guesthouse rather than a big hotel. I also save a few restaurants and cafés on my map app, but I don't plan every hour. The night before, I pack light, just one backpack, so I can move around easily. On the day of the trip, I get to the station a bit early and grab a snack for the ride. Honestly, that moment on the train is one of my favorite parts of traveling.

My family plans trips together, and we've kind of developed a system over the years. My older sister is in charge of finding a place to stay, because she's really good at comparing prices. I'm responsible for making the schedule, so I search for interesting places and good restaurants and put everything into a shared document. My dad takes care of the car, like checking the tires and filling up the gas tank. The night before we leave, we all pack our own bags, and my mom prepares fruit and snacks for the road. On the day of the trip, we leave before sunrise to avoid traffic, and we usually stop at a highway rest area for breakfast. Eating there is honestly one of the highlights of the whole trip.

ih.text: Planning a trip is actually one of my favorite parts of traveling, so I put quite a bit of effort into it. Usually about a month in advance, I choose a destination and then read travel blogs to see what the area is like. Once I've decided, I book my transportation right away. If I'm going somewhere far like Busan or Gangneung, I take the high-speed train, and those tickets can sell out fast on holidays. Next, I look for a place to stay, and I tend to choose places with good reviews about cleanliness rather than fancy facilities. About a week before the trip, I make a rough plan for each day, but I always leave some free time, because the best moments often come from things you don't plan. The night before, I pack light and double-check my tickets. On the morning of the trip, I'm usually so excited that I wake up before my alarm goes off.
phrases: put quite a bit of effort into it

ih.text: My routine before a trip in Korea is pretty relaxed, but there are a few things I always do. First, I check the weather forecast carefully, because it can completely change what I pack and what I can do. For example, if it's going to rain, I look for indoor places like museums or markets. Then I book a place to stay, usually through an app, and I always read the most recent reviews. I don't plan every detail, but I do make a list of a few local foods I want to try, since eating is honestly the main reason I travel. The night before, I pack a small suitcase with comfortable shoes, a power bank, and a light jacket, because evenings near the sea can get chilly. On the day of the trip, I leave early so I have a full day at my destination.
phrases: there are a few things I always do

al.text: I'd describe myself as a planner, so my preparation for a trip in Korea starts well before I actually leave. The first step is choosing where to go, and I usually decide based on the season. In spring I like places known for cherry blossoms, in summer the east coast, and in autumn somewhere with mountains and colorful leaves. Once I've settled on a destination, I immediately book train tickets, because if you wait until the last minute, especially around long weekends, you might end up standing in the aisle for hours. Then I look for a place to stay, and I've learned the hard way that a cheap place far from everything isn't really a bargain, so I put location first. After that, I put together a loose plan in a notes app, with a few must-see spots, restaurants, and backup options in case of bad weather. The night before, I pack as light as possible, usually just a backpack, and I charge every device I own. On the day itself, I like to get to the station early, buy a coffee, and just enjoy that feeling of the trip finally beginning.
phrases: I'd describe myself as a planner

al.text: Funnily enough, my approach to preparing for trips has become much simpler over time. These days, when I travel somewhere in Korea, I really only take care of three things in advance: transportation, a place to stay, and one or two things I definitely want to do. For example, if I'm heading to Jeju, I'll book my flight and a rental car first, since those get expensive quickly, and then find a small guesthouse in an area I haven't explored yet. Beyond that, I leave the schedule open on purpose. I used to plan every hour, but I found that I spent the whole trip checking my watch instead of enjoying myself. Now, I'd rather ask the guesthouse owner for recommendations or just follow a street that looks interesting. As for packing, I keep a checklist on my phone so I don't forget things like chargers, medicine, or a power bank. On the day I leave, I always make sure to eat a proper breakfast, because I know that once I start exploring, I'll probably forget about lunch.

questions.tip_ko: 여행 몇 주 전 → 전날 → 당일 순서로 시간을 나눠 말하면 준비 과정을 빠짐없이 말할 수 있어요.

questions.question: Tell me about a memorable trip you took in your country. Where did you go, who were you with, and what happened that made the trip so special? Give me as many details as you can.

il.text: Last year, I went to Busan with my friends. We went to the beach. We swam in the sea. At night, we ate seafood. It was very delicious. We took many pictures. It was a great trip.
Two years ago, I went to Jeju Island with my family. We rented a car. We climbed a mountain. It was hard but fun. We ate black pork. I want to go there again with my family.

im1.text: Last summer, I went to Gangneung with my two best friends. We took the train from Seoul. When we arrived, we went to the beach right away. The water was cold, but we swam anyway. In the evening, we ate fresh seafood near the beach. The next morning, we woke up early and watched the sunrise. It was so beautiful. It was my favorite trip ever.

I remember a trip to Gyeongju when I was in high school. It was a school trip, so I went with all my classmates. We visited old temples and museums. Honestly, I was bored during the day. But at night, my friends and I talked and laughed until very late in our room. The teacher got angry at us. Now it is a funny memory for me.

im2.text: One trip I'll never forget is when I went to Jeju Island with my family three years ago. It was the first time we traveled together in a long time, because my brother and I were busy with work. We rented a car and drove around the island for four days. On the second day, we decided to climb Hallasan. It was much harder than we expected, and my dad almost gave up. But we helped each other and finally reached the top. The view was amazing. That evening, we ate black pork barbecue and talked about the climb for hours. It was a really special trip for all of us.

I had a memorable trip to Busan last fall. I went alone for the first time, so I was a little nervous. On the first day, I visited a fish market and tried raw fish, which was so fresh. In the evening, I walked along the beach and saw a big fireworks festival. I didn't even know about the festival before I went, so it was a lucky surprise. Thousands of people were watching, and the sky was full of colors. After that trip, I realized traveling alone can be really fun, and now I do it once or twice a year.

im3.text: The most memorable trip I've taken in Korea was a weekend in Jeonju with my college friends. We had planned the trip for months, but when we arrived, it was pouring rain. At first, we were really disappointed, because we had planned to walk around the hanok village all day. Then one of my friends had an idea. We rented traditional clothes anyway and borrowed umbrellas from the shop. Walking through the old alleys in the rain, wearing hanbok, turned out to be really fun, and the photos looked amazing because there were hardly any other tourists. In the evening, we ate bibimbap in a tiny restaurant where the owner told us stories about the city. Looking back, the rain actually made that trip special.

I'd like to talk about a trip to Sokcho that I took with my parents last autumn. It was my dad's sixtieth birthday, so my sister and I planned the whole trip as a surprise. We booked a hotel with an ocean view and made a reservation at a nice seafood restaurant. On the second day, we hiked part of Seoraksan, and the leaves were bright red and orange. My mom kept stopping to take pictures, so it took us twice as long as we planned. In the evening, we gave my dad a small cake and a letter we had written. He didn't say much, but I could see he was really moved. It was the first time I felt like I was giving something back to my parents.
phrases: it took us twice as long

ih.text: Let me tell you about a trip that didn't go as planned but turned out to be unforgettable. About two years ago, my friend and I visited Jeju Island in early spring. We had everything planned, from our rental car to the restaurants we wanted to try. But on the very first day, a big storm hit the island, and most outdoor places were closed. We were stuck in our guesthouse, feeling pretty miserable. Then the owner, an older woman who had lived on Jeju her whole life, invited us to make dumplings with her family in the kitchen. She told us stories about how the island had changed over the years, and her husband taught us a traditional card game. By the time the storm passed two days later, we felt like part of the family. We still keep in touch, and that trip taught me that the people you meet matter more than the places you see.
phrases: we felt like part of the family

ih.text: The most memorable trip I've had in Korea was a road trip along the east coast with my college roommate right after we graduated. We borrowed her parents' old car and drove all the way down to Busan over five days, stopping in small towns along the way. We didn't book anything in advance, so every night we had to look for a place to stay, which was a little stressful but also exciting. One night in a tiny fishing village, all the guesthouses were full, and we ended up sleeping in the car near the beach. We woke up to the most incredible sunrise I've ever seen, with fishing boats heading out to sea. When we finally reached Busan, we were exhausted and our clothes smelled terrible, but we were so proud of ourselves. That trip marked the end of our student life, and it still feels like one of the best decisions we ever made.
phrases: We didn't book anything in advance
we ended up sleeping in the car

al.text: I'd have to say the most memorable trip I've taken in Korea was a solo trip to Gyeongju during a really difficult period in my life. I had just quit a job that I'd been unhappy at for a long time, and I was feeling lost and a bit anxious about the future. On a whim, I bought a train ticket and booked a small guesthouse near the old town for three nights. I didn't make any plans at all. Each morning, I rented a bike and just rode around, stopping wherever something caught my eye. One afternoon, I ended up sitting next to one of the huge royal tombs for almost two hours, just watching families having picnics and kids rolling down the grass. It sounds simple, but being surrounded by things that had stood there for over a thousand years made my own worries feel much smaller. On the last evening, I visited the old palace pond when it was lit up, and I remember thinking that everything was going to be okay. A few weeks later, I started a new job that I actually enjoy, and I still think of that trip as a kind of turning point.

One trip that really stands out is a family trip to Busan we took the winter my grandmother turned eighty. She had grown up near the port there but hadn't been back in almost fifty years, so the whole family decided to take her. We rode the high-speed train down together, three generations in one row of seats, and she spent the whole ride telling us stories we'd never heard before. Once we arrived, she wanted to go to the old fish market first. Of course, it had completely changed, and at first she seemed a little disappointed. But then she found a small stall run by a woman who, it turned out, had known her family decades ago. The two of them started crying and laughing at the same time, and we all just stood there in shock. We spent the rest of the afternoon at that tiny stall, eating grilled fish and listening to them catch up. It wasn't the kind of trip with famous sights or perfect photos, but it's the one my family still talks about every holiday.
phrases: It wasn't the kind of trip

questions.tip_ko: 누구와 갔는지, 예상과 달랐던 일 하나를 중심으로 이야기해요. 문제가 생겼다가 풀린 이야기는 높은 등급 답변에 특히 잘 어울려요.

questions.question: Compare the trips you took in your country when you were a child with the trips you take now. How are they different, and what do you think caused those changes?

il.text: When I was a child, I traveled with my parents. We went by car. Now I travel with my friends. We go by train. Before, I went to the beach. Now I like cities more.
In the past, my family went camping a lot. We slept in a tent. Now I stay in a hotel. It is more comfortable. But I miss camping with my family very much.

im1.text: When I was a child, my family traveled in Korea every summer. We always went to the beach by car, and the traffic was terrible. My parents planned everything. Now I travel with my friends, and we usually take the train because it is fast. I also plan the trips myself. I think the biggest change is that I have more freedom now, but I miss my family trips.

In the past, I traveled only during school vacations. My parents chose the places, and we usually visited my grandparents in the countryside. Now I travel when I want, maybe three or four times a year. I like to visit new cities and try local food. I also use my phone to find places. In the past, we used a paper map. Traveling is much easier now.
phrases: Now I travel when I want

im2.text: My trips have changed a lot since I was a child. When I was young, my family went on a trip once a year during summer vacation. We always drove to the beach, and it took a very long time because of traffic. We stayed in a cheap room and ate instant noodles a lot. These days, I travel more often, maybe four or five times a year. I usually take the train and stay at nice guesthouses. I also spend more money on food. I think these changes happened because I have my own income now, and transportation in Korea has become much faster and more convenient.
phrases: I think these changes happened because

im2.text: There are some big differences between my childhood trips and my trips now. When I was a kid, trips were all about playing. I swam at the beach, built sandcastles, and caught bugs in the mountains. I didn't care about history or food at all. Now I'm more interested in culture and local food, so I visit museums, old villages, and traditional markets. Another difference is how I find information. My parents used guidebooks and asked people for directions, but I use my smartphone for everything. I think I've changed because I'm older and more curious about the places I visit.

im3.text: Comparing my childhood trips with the trips I take now, I'd say the biggest difference is who makes the decisions. When I was young, my parents decided everything, and we usually went to the same beach town every summer because my dad liked it. I remember sitting in the back seat for hours, fighting with my brother. Nowadays, I plan my own trips, and I prefer going to new places I've never been to, like small towns with interesting history. I also travel by train much more, because it's faster and I can relax instead of driving. Another change is the season. I used to travel only in the summer, but now I actually prefer spring and fall, since it's not as hot or crowded.

My trips in Korea used to be completely different. When I was in elementary school, my family went camping almost every month. My dad loved it, so we'd drive to a campsite near a river or a mountain, set up a big tent, and cook meat on a grill. At the time, I thought it was really fun, even though the bugs were terrible. These days, I hardly ever camp. I usually stay in a hotel or a guesthouse, and I spend more time in cafés, museums, and markets than in nature. I think part of the reason is that I'm busier now, so I want my trips to be comfortable and relaxing. Still, every time I smell a campfire, I miss those family weekends.
phrases: part of the reason is that

ih.text: When I think about the trips I took as a child compared to now, the difference is pretty dramatic. Back then, travel in Korea meant one big trip every summer. My whole family would squeeze into our small car and drive to the east coast, which took about seven or eight hours because of the traffic. We'd stay in a crowded room near the beach and eat simple meals we cooked ourselves to save money. Today, things couldn't be more different. With the high-speed train, I can get to the coast in a couple of hours, so I go on short weekend trips several times a year instead of one long one. I also pay much more attention to food and atmosphere, and I'll happily spend money on a nice meal or a guesthouse with a view. I think these changes come from better transportation and the fact that I'm earning my own money.

There's a big difference between how I traveled as a kid and how I travel now, mainly in terms of what I look for in a trip. When I was a child, my parents mostly took us to famous tourist spots, like big amusement parks or well-known beaches. Everything was planned around keeping my sister and me entertained, so we spent a lot of time waiting in lines. Now, I actually try to avoid crowded tourist spots. I prefer small towns, quiet hiking trails, and local markets where I can see how people really live. Another big change is technology. My parents relied on road maps and asked gas station workers for directions, but I can find almost everything I need on my phone in seconds. Honestly, I think that has made traveling easier, but maybe also a little less adventurous than it used to be.

al.text: Thinking back, the way I travel around Korea has changed almost completely since I was a kid, and I think it reflects how the country itself has changed. When I was young, a family trip was a major event. We'd go once a year, usually during the peak summer holiday, along with what felt like the entire country. I remember spending entire days stuck on the highway, eating snacks at rest areas, and arriving at a packed beach where it was hard to even find a spot for our umbrella. Our rooms were basic, and my parents carefully planned the cost of every meal. These days, travel feels much more casual and personal. Thanks to the high-speed train network, I can leave Seoul on a Friday evening and be by the sea in a couple of hours, so I take lots of short trips throughout the year, often in the off-season. I also tend to choose experiences over sightseeing, like a cooking class in a small town or a quiet stay in a traditional house. If I had to name the biggest reasons for the change, I'd say faster transportation, having my own income, and the fact that I've learned to value rest more than checking places off a list.

If I compare the trips I took as a child with the ones I take now, the most obvious difference is the role I play. As a kid, I was basically a passenger. My parents chose where we went, booked everything, and I just tagged along, usually complaining about being bored in the car. Most of our trips were to visit relatives in the countryside during the holidays, so they felt more like family duties than vacations. Now that I'm an adult, I'm the one making the decisions, and I've become a lot more thoughtful about where I go and why. I tend to pick places that have some kind of story, like an old port city or a village known for a traditional craft, and I do a bit of reading before I go so I can appreciate what I'm seeing. Interestingly, I've also started taking my parents on trips, which feels like a complete role reversal. Watching them enjoy a place I chose is probably the most rewarding part of traveling these days.

questions.tip_ko: When I was a child와 these days로 두 덩어리를 나눠 말하고, 차이마다 이유를 붙여요. 교통, 돈, 관심사의 변화가 이유로 쓰기 쉬워요.

questions.question: Let's talk about holidays. What are some of the biggest holidays in your country? Tell me about one of them. When is it, and what does it mean to people?

il.text: The biggest holidays in Korea are Seollal and Chuseok. Seollal is the Lunar New Year. It is in winter. People visit their family. We eat rice cake soup. It is a happy day.
Chuseok is a big holiday in Korea. It is in fall. People go to their hometown. We eat songpyeon. Songpyeon is a rice cake. I like Chuseok because I can rest.

im1.text: In Korea, we have two big holidays, Seollal and Chuseok. I want to talk about Seollal. Seollal is the Lunar New Year, so it is usually in January or February. On Seollal, families get together and eat tteokguk, rice cake soup. People say eating tteokguk makes you one year older. It is a very important day for families, and I always look forward to it.
phrases: It is a very important day

im1.text: There are many holidays in Korea, but the biggest one is Chuseok. It is a harvest holiday in the fall. Many people travel to their hometown to see their family. The roads are very busy at that time. We make songpyeon and share food together. For many Koreans, Chuseok means family and thanks. I usually stay with my grandparents for two or three days.

im2.text: Korea has a few big holidays, but I think the most important one is Chuseok. It's in September or October, and it's kind of like Thanksgiving. Long ago, people celebrated the harvest and thanked their ancestors. These days, most families still get together, make songpyeon, and share a big meal. The holiday usually lasts three days, so a lot of people travel to their hometowns. For me, Chuseok is a time to slow down and spend time with my grandparents. That's why it's special to me, and I never miss it.

Let me tell you about Seollal, the Lunar New Year. It's one of the two biggest holidays in Korea, and it usually falls in January or February. On the morning of Seollal, people wear nice clothes and bow to their parents and grandparents. Then the elders give them some money and good wishes for the new year. After that, everyone eats tteokguk together. I think Seollal is meaningful because it's a fresh start, and the whole family is together. Also, many families play traditional games like yunnori in the afternoon. It's always noisy but fun.
phrases: I think Seollal is meaningful because

im3.text: Well, in Korea there are two really big holidays, Seollal and Chuseok, and I'd like to talk about Chuseok. It comes in early fall, around September, when the weather is cool and clear. Traditionally, it was a festival to celebrate the harvest and remember our ancestors. On Chuseok, families gather at the oldest relative's house, prepare food together, and hold a small memorial ceremony. Children usually enjoy songpyeon, which are small half-moon rice cakes. Honestly, the traffic is terrible because everyone goes home at the same time. But I still love Chuseok, because it's one of the few times a year when my whole family is in one place. I really look forward to it every year.

One of the biggest holidays in my country is Seollal, which is the Lunar New Year. It usually comes in January or February, and the date changes every year because it follows the lunar calendar. Seollal is all about family and new beginnings. In the morning, younger people bow deeply to their elders, and the elders give them pocket money and words of advice. Then we sit down and eat tteokguk, rice cake soup. In the afternoon, we often play traditional games like yunnori. When I was a kid, I waited all year for Seollal because of the pocket money, but now I enjoy the relaxed time with my relatives more.

ih.text: Sure. Korea has several national holidays, but the two that really matter to most people are Seollal and Chuseok. I'd like to focus on Chuseok because I think it shows Korean culture well. Chuseok falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, so it's usually in September or early October. Historically, it was a harvest festival, a time to thank our ancestors for good crops. Even now, many families visit their ancestors' graves, clean the area, and hold a memorial ceremony with fresh fruit and rice cakes. Of course, things have changed a lot. In the past, the women in the family did almost all of the cooking, but these days more families share the work or just buy prepared food. Some people even use the long holiday to travel abroad. Still, for most Koreans, Chuseok is about being grateful and reconnecting with family.
phrases: Of course, things have changed a lot

ih.text: I'd say the biggest holiday in Korea is Seollal, the Lunar New Year. Most people get three days off, and the date moves around every year, but it's always in January or February. The heart of Seollal is a custom called sebae. Younger family members put on their best clothes, sometimes even hanbok, and bow to their elders to wish them a healthy new year. In return, the elders give them a little money and some advice. After that comes the food. Every family eats tteokguk, and there's a saying that you only get one year older after you finish your bowl. What I like about Seollal is that it feels like a second chance. If my January didn't go well, Seollal gives me another opportunity to start the year over with a clear mind. That's why I always try to make a new plan on that day.
phrases: What I like about Seollal is

al.text: Korea has quite a few public holidays, but if you ask anyone which ones matter most, they'll say Seollal and Chuseok without hesitation. I'd like to talk about Chuseok, which people often call Korean Thanksgiving. It's celebrated on the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the lunar calendar, so it usually lands in late September or early October, when the weather is at its best. At its core, Chuseok is a harvest festival. Families set up a table with newly harvested rice, fruit, and songpyeon to honor their ancestors, and many people visit family graves to clean them and pay their respects. What makes the holiday interesting, though, is how much it's changing. A generation ago, almost everyone squeezed onto crowded highways to reach their hometowns. Nowadays, it's not unusual for parents to come to their children's apartments in the city instead, or for young couples to spend the holiday traveling. So while the traditions are still there, I'd say the meaning of Chuseok is slowly shifting from duty toward simply spending quality time together.
phrases: What makes the holiday interesting, though

al.text: If I had to pick the most important holiday in my country, I'd go with Seollal, the Lunar New Year. Since it follows the lunar calendar, the date changes every year, but it always comes somewhere between late January and mid-February. For most families, the day begins early in the morning with a memorial ceremony for the ancestors, followed by sebae, where children and younger adults bow to their elders. The elders then hand out pocket money along with a few words of wisdom, which, to be honest, kids care much less about than the money. Then comes tteokguk, the rice cake soup that supposedly makes you one year older. Beyond the rituals, Seollal has a deeper meaning for Koreans. It's a moment to pause, look back on the previous year, and reconnect with relatives you might not have seen for months. In a society where people work such long hours, I think that pause is actually what makes the holiday so valuable. For me, it's the most meaningful day of the whole year, even more than my birthday.

questions.question: What do you usually do during the holidays? Walk me through a typical holiday for you, from the time you get up until the end of the day.

il.text: On holidays, I get up late. I eat breakfast with my family. Then I watch TV. In the afternoon, I meet my friends. At night, I play games. I go to bed late.
During Chuseok, I go to my grandmother's house. We cook food together. We eat a lot. Then we talk and watch movies. I sleep there. It is fun but tiring.
phrases: I go to my grandmother's house

im1.text: On a typical holiday, I wake up later than usual, maybe around ten. First, I have a big breakfast with my family. After that, we usually visit my grandparents. My mom and aunts cook a lot of food, and I help a little. In the evening, my cousins and I play board games or watch a movie. I usually go to bed very late, so the next day I am always tired.

During long holidays like Seollal, my day is usually the same. In the morning, I put on nice clothes and bow to my parents. Then we eat rice cake soup together. In the afternoon, we visit my uncle's house. We talk, eat fruit, and play cards. At night, I come home and relax in my room. I like this routine because it is calm and easy.
phrases: my day is usually the same

im2.text: On holidays, my routine changes a lot from my normal weekday routine. First of all, I don't set an alarm, so I usually sleep until about ten. After a slow breakfast, my family drives to my grandparents' house, which takes about two hours. When we arrive, everyone starts preparing food. I'm in charge of making jeon, the Korean pancakes, because my grandmother says I'm good at it. In the afternoon, we eat together and talk about what happened during the year. In the evening, my cousins and I usually go out for coffee. Honestly, it's tiring, but I enjoy it.

To be honest, my holiday routine is pretty simple. Since my family lives nearby, I don't have to travel far. In the morning, I have breakfast with my parents and help them clean the house. Around lunchtime, my relatives come over, and we eat a big meal together. After lunch, the adults talk and the younger people play games on their phones. Later in the afternoon, I usually take a walk around the neighborhood because I eat too much. At night, I watch a holiday movie on TV. It's a quiet routine, but I like it.

im3.text: Well, I usually spend the holidays at my parents' house, so my routine is pretty fixed. I get up a bit earlier than I'd like, around eight, because my mom starts cooking early. After a quick breakfast, I help her prepare dishes for the family meal. My job is usually chopping vegetables and frying jeon, which takes almost the whole morning. Around noon, my aunts and uncles arrive, and the house suddenly becomes really loud. We eat lunch together and catch up on each other's news. In the afternoon, the older relatives take a nap, and my cousins and I go for a walk or play yunnori. By evening, everyone leaves, and I finally collapse on the sofa. It's exhausting, but I'd miss it if I didn't do it.
phrases: I'd miss it if I didn't

im3.text: These days, my holiday routine is quite different from when I was younger. Now that I live alone, I usually spend the first day of the holiday resting. I sleep in, order delivery food, and catch up on dramas I missed. On the second day, I take the train to my hometown, which is about three hours away. When I get there, I spend time with my parents, help with the cooking, and visit my grandparents' graves with them. On the last day, I go back to the city a little early to avoid the traffic. I think this routine works well for me, because I can rest and still see my family.

ih.text: My holiday routine depends a little on which holiday it is, but for Chuseok it's almost always the same. The day before the holiday, my family drives to my grandmother's house in the countryside. We leave very early in the morning, around five, because otherwise we'd be stuck in traffic for hours. As soon as we arrive, the kitchen turns into a busy restaurant. My mother and aunts make the main dishes, and my cousins and I are in charge of frying pancakes and making songpyeon. On the morning of Chuseok, we hold a short memorial ceremony for our ancestors, and then we have a huge breakfast together. In the afternoon, we usually visit the family graves on a hill nearby. After that, the rest of the day is pretty relaxed. We play cards, watch TV, and eat leftovers. It's tiring, but it's also the only time I really feel connected to my extended family.
phrases: After that, the rest of the day

ih.text: Honestly, over the last few years my holiday routine has changed quite a bit. When I was in school, holidays meant long car trips and lots of cooking at my grandparents' house. But since my grandmother moved in with my uncle in Seoul, our family gatherings have become much shorter and simpler. Now, on a typical holiday, I wake up around nine and have breakfast with my parents. Around eleven, we drive to my uncle's apartment, which is only thirty minutes away. We eat lunch together, and instead of cooking everything from scratch, we buy some dishes from a local market. In the afternoon, we take a walk along the river, which has become a new family tradition. Then I usually go home in the early evening and spend the rest of the holiday on my own, reading or meeting friends. I actually prefer this routine because everyone is less stressed.
phrases: I actually prefer this routine because

al.text: My holidays tend to follow a pretty predictable pattern, and I've come to appreciate that. The night before, I pack a small bag and set my alarm for some ridiculous hour like four-thirty, because the only way to beat holiday traffic is to leave before everyone else does. By the time the sun comes up, we're usually halfway to my grandparents' village. Once we arrive, there's no time to rest. My grandmother hands out jobs the moment we walk in, and mine has been the same for about ten years: frying fish and vegetable pancakes in a giant pan on the floor of the veranda. That takes most of the morning, and by lunchtime I smell like cooking oil. The afternoon is more relaxed. We eat together, and then the adults drink tea and talk about relatives I've never met, while the younger cousins disappear to the convenience store. In the evening, we play yunnori, which always gets surprisingly competitive. It's exhausting, but if I skipped it, the holiday just wouldn't feel like a holiday.
phrases: tend to follow a pretty predictable pattern
Once we arrive, there's no time to rest

al.text: For me, holidays are split into two very different parts, and I plan them that way on purpose. The first half belongs to my family. On the first morning, I go to my parents' place, and we follow the usual customs. We prepare a simple table for our ancestors, bow to my grandparents, and then sit down for a long breakfast. My parents always ask about my job and whether I'm eating properly, which I've learned to answer with a smile. After lunch, we usually go to a nearby park or a café, just to get out of the house. The second half of the holiday, though, is for me. I go back to my apartment, turn off my work notifications, and do things I never have time for during the year. Sometimes that means finishing a novel in one sitting, and sometimes it's a long bike ride along the river. I've found that balancing family time with some time alone makes me feel much more rested when I go back to work.
phrases: are split into two very different parts
The second half of the holiday, though

questions.tip_ko: 아침 → 점심 → 오후 → 저녁 순서로 시간 표현(In the morning, After that)을 붙이면 길게 말해도 흐름이 끊기지 않아요.

questions.question: Tell me about a memorable holiday you had. When was it, who were you with, and what happened? Why do you still remember it?

il.text: Last Chuseok was special. I went to Busan with my family. We ate seafood. We walked on the beach. The weather was very good. I was very happy. I remember it well.
Two years ago, I was alone on Seollal. I had to work. I ate ramen at home. I called my parents on the phone. I was sad. So I remember this holiday.

im1.text: I remember the Chuseok when I was ten years old. My whole family went to my grandmother's house in the countryside. There was a big full moon that night. My grandmother told us to make a wish. I wished for a new bike. A few weeks later, my dad bought me a bike. It was just luck, but I still remember that night.

My most memorable holiday was Seollal three years ago. That year, I traveled to Japan with my friends instead of going home. It was my first holiday without my family. We ate a lot of good food and went to a hot spring. It was fun, but I missed my mom's rice cake soup. Since then, I always go home for Seollal.

im2.text: I still remember the Seollal when I was in high school. That year, it snowed a lot, and my family couldn't drive to my grandparents' house. At first, everyone was disappointed. My mom was worried because she bought a lot of food for the whole family. So we decided to have a video call with my grandparents and bow to them through the screen. It felt strange, but also really funny. After that, we cooked all the food ourselves and invited our neighbors. It became one of the warmest holidays I've ever had, and that's why I can't forget it.
phrases: that's why I can't forget it

im2.text: The most memorable holiday for me was Chuseok last year, because it was the first time I cooked for my family. My mom hurt her wrist a week before the holiday, so she couldn't cook. I watched a lot of cooking videos and made jeon, japchae, and soup. Honestly, some dishes were too salty, and the kitchen was a mess. But my grandparents said it was delicious, and my mom looked really proud. I felt like I grew up a little that day. That's why that Chuseok is still special to me.
phrases: because it was the first time

im3.text: Let me tell you about the Chuseok I spent in Canada about four years ago. I was an exchange student there, so I couldn't go home for the holiday. I felt pretty lonely at first, because I could see photos of my family's dinner on social media. Then a few other Korean students and I decided to have our own Chuseok party. We found rice cake powder at an Asian market and tried to make songpyeon, but they all looked terrible. We also invited our Canadian roommates and explained what Chuseok means. They loved the food, even the ugly rice cakes. That night, I realized that a holiday is really about the people around you, not the place. I still keep in touch with those friends.
phrases: I felt pretty lonely at first

im3.text: The holiday I remember most is a Seollal from when I was about twelve. Early in the morning, my cousins and I bowed to our grandparents, and we got more pocket money than ever before. We were so excited that we went to a big stationery store together and spent almost all of it in one hour. When we came back, our parents were really upset, and they made us write down everything we bought. It was embarrassing, but it actually taught me a lesson about money. Since then, I always save at least half of my holiday money. Whenever my family gets together, someone still brings up that story and we all laugh about it.

ih.text: One holiday I'll never forget happened about five years ago during Chuseok. My family was driving to my grandparents' house, which normally takes three hours. But that year, there was a big accident on the highway, and we were stuck in traffic for almost nine hours. At first, everyone was annoyed, and my younger brother kept complaining that he was hungry. Then my dad suggested that we get off the highway and take the small country roads instead. It took longer, but we drove past rice fields and little villages, and we even stopped at a local market to buy roasted chestnuts. By the time we arrived, it was almost midnight, but my grandmother was waiting outside with a flashlight. Looking back, that long trip turned out to be one of my favorite family memories. It taught me that the unplanned parts of a holiday are often the best.

The most memorable holiday for me was the first Seollal after my grandfather passed away, which was about three years ago. Our family was nervous about it because he had always been the center of every holiday. He used to give the longest speeches during sebae and tell the same old stories every year. That morning, the house felt really quiet. But then my grandmother took out an old photo album, and we started looking at pictures from past holidays. Soon everyone was sharing funny stories about him, and we were laughing and crying at the same time. Instead of feeling empty, the day felt warm. Ever since then, we've made it a tradition to look at that album every Seollal. I remember that holiday because it showed me how strong my family is when we're together. I'm still really grateful for that day, even though it was sad.
phrases: which was about three years ago

al.text: A holiday that really stands out in my memory is the Chuseok when my family decided, for the first time ever, not to go to my grandparents' house. My grandparents had moved into a smaller apartment, and they suggested that we all meet at a beach town on the east coast instead. My parents were a little uneasy about breaking tradition, and honestly, so was I. We still prepared a simple memorial table in the guesthouse, but the rest of the trip was completely different from any holiday we'd had before. Instead of spending hours in a hot kitchen, we ate grilled fish at a small restaurant by the harbor, and in the evening the whole family sat on the beach and watched the full moon rise over the water. My grandfather, who almost never talks about his feelings, said it was the most relaxing Chuseok of his life. That moment changed the way I think about traditions. I used to believe they had to be followed exactly, but now I think the real point is simply to keep the family together, however you choose to do it.
phrases: really stands out in my memory
That moment changed the way I think about

al.text: I'd have to say the most memorable holiday I've had was last Seollal, mainly because almost nothing went according to plan. I'd volunteered to host my family at my new apartment for the first time, and I was determined to make everything perfect. The night before, I spent hours preparing tteokguk broth and pancakes. Then, early on the morning of Seollal, the power went out in my entire building. No stove, no heating, nothing. For a moment, I honestly thought the whole day was ruined. But my relatives handled it surprisingly well. My uncle went out and bought a portable gas burner, my cousins brought blankets, and we ended up eating rice cake soup in our coats by candlelight. It sounds miserable, but it was actually the most fun we'd had together in years, because everyone was joking and helping out. Looking back, I realize I'd been so focused on making things perfect that I'd forgotten what the holiday is really about. Now, whenever I host a family event, I try to relax and remember that the people matter more than the plan.
phrases: For a moment, I honestly thought

questions.tip_ko: 언제, 누구와, 무슨 일이 있었는지 과거형으로 말하고, 마지막에 왜 기억에 남는지 한 문장으로 정리해요.

questions.question: How have holidays in your country changed compared to when you were a child? What do people do differently now, and why do you think things have changed?

il.text: When I was a child, holidays were big. Many people came to my grandma's house. Now, we are small. We buy food. We do not cook a lot. People are busy now.
Before, people went to their hometown. The roads were busy. Now, many people travel. Some people go to other countries. I think it is because people want to rest and relax more.

im1.text: When I was young, holidays were very busy. All my relatives came to my grandmother's house, and we cooked for two days. Now, things are different. My family is smaller, and we buy some food from the store. Also, many young people travel during the holidays. I think things changed because people are busy and want to rest. I miss the old holidays a little.

Holidays in Korea changed a lot. In the past, everyone went to their hometown, and the roads were full of cars. These days, many parents visit their children in the city. Some families even go on a trip together. Also, people use video calls to say hello. I think technology and busy lives changed our holidays. I like the new way better.
phrases: I like the new way better

im2.text: Compared to when I was a child, holidays have become much simpler. Back then, my grandmother cooked for days, and around twenty relatives came to her house. Everyone had to follow the traditions exactly. Now, my family usually meets for just one meal, and we buy a lot of the food. Many of my friends even go abroad during long holidays. I think the biggest reason is that families are smaller and people are busier. Also, younger people care more about rest than tradition. Personally, I think the change is natural, but I hope we don't lose the meaning of the holidays.
phrases: Compared to when I was a child
I think the biggest reason is

im2.text: Holidays have changed a lot since I was little. When I was a child, the whole country seemed to move at the same time, and highways were completely full. These days, traffic is still bad, but many people choose to stay home or travel instead. Another big change is the food. In the past, women in the family did almost all the cooking, but now men help more, and many families order dishes. I think these changes happened because people's values changed. Now, people think holidays should be relaxing for everyone, not just some people.
phrases: I think these changes happened because

im3.text: I'd say holidays in Korea have changed quite a lot since I was a kid. When I was young, Seollal and Chuseok were all about big family gatherings. We'd spend hours in traffic, and once we arrived, the women would cook all day while the men talked. Nowadays, families are smaller, and a lot of people live far from their hometowns, so gatherings are shorter. Many families buy prepared food or eat at restaurants. Some people even take the long holiday as a chance to travel overseas. I think there are two main reasons. First, people are much busier and more tired than before. Second, younger generations think holidays should be fair and relaxing for everyone. I think it's a positive change overall.
phrases: have changed quite a lot since
I think there are two main reasons

im3.text: Compared to my childhood, holidays today feel more flexible. Back then, there was one right way to celebrate, and every family followed it. My grandfather was very strict about the memorial ceremony, and we had to prepare more than twenty dishes. These days, my family still does the ceremony, but it's much simpler, with just a few dishes. Also, instead of everyone traveling to my grandparents' house, they sometimes come to Seoul to see us. Another change is that people share holiday greetings online instead of visiting every relative. I think the main reason for these changes is that society has become more individual, and people respect each other's time more. Honestly, I like the new style better.
phrases: Honestly, I like the new style better

ih.text: When I compare holidays now with the holidays I remember from my childhood, the biggest difference is how much smaller and more flexible they've become. When I was little, Chuseok meant a long trip to the countryside, a house packed with relatives, and a mountain of food that took two full days to prepare. The rules were strict, and nobody would ever think of skipping the memorial ceremony. These days, my extended family rarely gathers all at once. Some relatives come for lunch and leave early, and a few of my cousins spend the holiday traveling abroad instead. Even the food has changed, since many families now order holiday dishes online. In my opinion, there are a few reasons for this. Families are smaller, more people live alone, and younger generations question traditions that put too much work on certain family members. I don't think the holidays have lost their meaning. They've just adapted to the way people live now.
phrases: In my opinion, there are a few reasons for this

ih.text: Holidays in Korea have gone through a big transformation over the last twenty years or so. When I was a child, I remember everything being about obligation. You had to go to your hometown, you had to bow to every relative, and the women in the family had to cook nonstop. People complained, but nobody really questioned it. Nowadays, the atmosphere is completely different. Many families divide the cooking evenly or simply buy prepared food, and it's common to visit the in-laws on one holiday and your own parents on the next. There are even people who spend the entire holiday on a trip with friends. I think this change comes from two things. First, younger Koreans value equality and personal time much more. Second, the population has moved to big cities, so hometown visits feel less natural. Personally, I think the new style is healthier for families.
phrases: have gone through a big transformation
Nowadays, the atmosphere is completely different
I think this change comes from two things

al.text: Looking back, I'd say holidays in Korea have changed more in the last twenty years than in the previous hundred. When I was a child, a holiday like Chuseok followed a very fixed script. Everyone traveled to the eldest son's house, no matter how far it was, and the day revolved around the ancestral ceremony, which required an enormous amount of food. The work was rarely shared equally, and honestly, a lot of people, especially women, dreaded the holidays. Today, the picture is much more varied. Some families still keep every tradition, but many have simplified the ceremony or dropped it entirely. It's become common to order the holiday food, to meet at a restaurant instead of someone's home, or to use the long break for a vacation. I think the changes come from a mix of factors. Families are smaller and more scattered, people are more aware of gender equality, and the younger generation doesn't feel that tradition alone is a good enough reason to do something. Personally, I see it as a healthy evolution, as long as people still make time for their families.
phrases: Today, the picture is much more varied
I see it as a healthy evolution

al.text: The way Koreans spend their holidays has shifted dramatically since I was a kid, and you can see it almost everywhere. Back then, the main image of Chuseok on the news was endless traffic jams and train stations packed with people carrying gift boxes. The whole country seemed to be heading home at once, and families followed the same routine: cook, perform the ceremony, eat, and repeat. Nowadays, the news is just as likely to show crowded airports, because a huge number of people treat the holiday as a chance to travel. Even families that stay home have adjusted things. My aunt, for example, used to insist on making everything from scratch, but a few years ago she announced that we'd be ordering half of the dishes, and nobody complained. In my view, these changes reflect larger trends in society. People work longer hours, they live farther from their parents, and they're more willing to question customs that cause stress. I don't think we've lost anything essential, though. If anything, holidays feel more relaxed and genuine now.
phrases: In my view, these changes reflect

questions.question: Some people say holiday travel and family gatherings cause a lot of stress, and many people now skip them. What do you think about this issue? Why do people feel this way, and what could be done about it?

il.text: I think holidays are stressful. People drive a long time. They cook a lot. Some people fight. So some people stay home and rest. I think families should cook less and talk more.
Many people do not like holidays now. They are tired. The traffic is bad. Relatives ask many questions. I think we can meet for a short time. That is better.

im1.text: I think many people feel stress during holidays. First, the traffic is terrible, so traveling takes a long time. Second, there is a lot of cooking, and usually only some family members do it. Also, relatives often ask personal questions about jobs or marriage. Because of this, some people stay home. I think families should share the work and not ask too many personal questions.
phrases: I think many people feel stress

im1.text: These days, many young people skip family gatherings, and I understand why. Holidays are supposed to be relaxing, but they are often very tiring. People spend many hours on the road. They also feel pressure from older relatives. I think the solution is to make holidays simple. For example, families can meet for one meal and order food. Then everyone can enjoy the time together.

im2.text: I think holiday stress is a real problem in Korea. There are a few reasons. First, traveling to your hometown can take many hours because everyone goes at the same time. Second, preparing traditional food is a lot of work, and in many families, the women still do most of it. Third, some relatives ask personal questions, like when you will get married or how much money you make. Because of all this, more people are skipping family gatherings. In my opinion, families should talk openly and decide together how to celebrate. For example, they can share the cooking or meet in a restaurant.
phrases: is a real problem in Korea

im2.text: To be honest, I can understand why many people find holidays stressful. Holidays should be a time to rest, but for a lot of people, they feel like extra work. You have to drive for hours, cook all day, and answer uncomfortable questions from relatives. On top of that, some people feel guilty if they don't follow every tradition. I think the answer is not to stop meeting family, but to change the way we celebrate. My family started meeting for just one day and buying some of the food. Since then, everyone has been much happier.
phrases: To be honest, I can understand why
I think the answer is not to

im3.text: Holiday stress has become a pretty common topic in Korea, and I think it's a serious issue. Every year, you see news stories about family arguments and even divorces after long holidays. I think there are several reasons. First, the traditional way of celebrating requires a huge amount of work, and it's often not shared fairly. Second, holiday travel is exhausting because the whole country moves at once. Third, many young people feel pressure from relatives who compare them with others. Because of this, a lot of people now choose to stay home or travel alone. To solve this, I think families need to update their traditions. For example, they could simplify the ceremony, share the cooking, and avoid sensitive questions. Holidays should be enjoyable for everyone.
phrases: has become a pretty common topic
I think there are several reasons

im3.text: I personally think it's natural that more people are skipping holiday gatherings. Many traditions were created when most people lived in the same village and families were much bigger. Now, people live far away from their hometowns and work long hours, so a long trip during a short holiday can be really tiring. Also, younger people don't like being asked about their grades, jobs, or marriage plans in front of everyone. However, I don't think skipping family completely is the best answer. Instead, families could try new ways to get together, like meeting in the middle, or choosing a different weekend when traffic is lighter. If everyone is a little flexible, holidays can become something people look forward to again.
phrases: I personally think it's natural that
If everyone is a little flexible

ih.text: Holiday stress is definitely a real issue in Korea, and I think it has become more visible in recent years. On paper, holidays are about rest and family, but for many people, they mean long hours in traffic, endless cooking, and awkward conversations. A big part of the problem is that the traditional way of celebrating was designed for large families living close together, and it doesn't fit modern life very well. Another issue is fairness. In many households, the cooking and cleaning still fall mostly on women, which naturally creates tension. And for younger people, being questioned about their jobs or relationships in front of the whole family can be really uncomfortable. That's why more and more people are skipping gatherings or traveling instead. In my opinion, the solution isn't to abandon family holidays but to redesign them. Families could simplify the ceremonies, divide the work fairly, and agree to avoid sensitive topics. Small changes like that could make a big difference.
phrases: A big part of the problem is that
That's why more and more people
In my opinion, the solution isn't to

ih.text: I think it's important to talk about this issue honestly, because holiday stress affects a lot of families. From what I've seen, there are three main causes. The first is physical exhaustion. Traveling across the country on the same day as millions of other people is tiring before the holiday even starts. The second is the workload. Traditional holiday meals involve dozens of dishes, and the person who does most of the work often ends up resenting the whole event. The third is emotional pressure, especially for young adults who get compared with their cousins. Personally, I don't blame people for skipping gatherings, but I also think something valuable gets lost when they do. A better approach would be for families to openly discuss what they actually want from the holiday. In my family, we did that a few years ago, and we decided to cut the number of dishes in half and take turns hosting. Since then, holidays have become something we actually look forward to.
phrases: From what I've seen, there are three main causes
Personally, I don't blame people for

al.text: Holiday stress is a topic that comes up every single year in Korea, and I think it reflects a deeper gap between tradition and modern life. The customs we follow on Seollal and Chuseok developed when most people lived in farming villages with large extended families nearby. In that context, gathering at the eldest son's house and preparing a big ceremony made sense. Today, though, families are scattered across the country, most people work long hours, and the idea that certain family members should do all the cooking is increasingly seen as unfair. When you put all that together, it's no surprise that many people associate holidays with exhaustion rather than rest. Personally, I understand why some choose to skip gatherings altogether, but I think that's more of a symptom than a solution. What families really need is an honest conversation about which traditions still matter to them and which ones are just habits. For instance, some families have kept the memorial ceremony but stopped preparing dozens of dishes, while others have started rotating who hosts. If more people were willing to adapt like that, I think holidays could become meaningful again rather than something to survive.
phrases: more of a symptom than a solution

al.text: I think this issue is more complicated than it first appears. On one hand, the complaints about holiday stress are completely valid. Spending eight hours on the highway, cooking from dawn until night, and fielding personal questions about your salary or marriage plans is not most people's idea of a vacation. It's also worth noting that the burden has never been shared equally, and younger generations are much less willing to accept that. On the other hand, holidays are one of the few times when families actually sit down together, and in a society where everyone is so busy, that time is hard to replace. So rather than seeing it as a choice between keeping traditions and abandoning them, I think we should look for a middle ground. The government and companies could help by encouraging people to spread their vacation days around the holidays, which would ease traffic. Families, meanwhile, could agree on simpler meals and fairer roles. In the end, a holiday should leave people feeling closer to each other, not more exhausted, and I believe that's achievable with a bit of flexibility.
phrases: more complicated than it first appears
rather than seeing it as a choice between

questions.tip_ko: 이슈 문항은 '내 입장 → 이유 두세 개 → 해결 방법' 순서로 말해요. In my opinion, That's why 같은 연결어로 논리를 이어요.

questions.question: You indicated in the survey that you live in a house or an apartment. Please describe your home to me. What does it look like, and what rooms does it have? Which room do you like the most, and why?

il.text: I live in an apartment. It is on the tenth floor. It has two bedrooms and one bathroom. The living room is small. I like my bedroom. It is quiet. My bed is very comfortable. I like my home.
My home is a small house. There is a kitchen, a living room, and three bedrooms. My favorite room is the kitchen. It is big and bright. My family eats dinner there. I love my house.

im1.text: I live in an apartment with my family. It is not very big, but it is clean and bright. There are three bedrooms, two bathrooms, a kitchen, and a living room. My favorite room is my bedroom because it is my own space. I have a desk, a bed, and a big window there. At night, I can see the city lights from my window. I feel relaxed when I am in my room.
phrases: because it is my own space

im1.text: I live alone in a studio apartment near my office. It is only one room, so the kitchen, bed, and desk are all together. It is small, but I like it. My favorite place is the corner by the window. I put a small sofa and a plant there. After work, I sit on the sofa and listen to music. It is the most comfortable place for me.
phrases: It is small, but I like it

im2.text: Well, I live in an apartment with two roommates. It's on the fifth floor of an old building, so there's no elevator, which is kind of tiring. When you walk in, there's a long hallway, and on the right side there's a living room with a big gray sofa. We have three bedrooms, one for each of us, and we share a kitchen and a bathroom. My favorite room is actually the living room. In the evening, we often sit there together, watch TV, and talk about our day. It makes the apartment feel like a real home.
phrases: It makes the apartment feel like

im2.text: Okay, I live in a two-story house with my parents. On the first floor, there's a living room, a kitchen, and my parents' bedroom. On the second floor, there are two bedrooms, and one of them is mine. I like my room the most because it has a small balcony. I put some flower pots and a little chair out there. On weekends, I sit on the balcony with a cup of coffee and read a book. It's quiet and peaceful, so it's the best place to relax in my house.
phrases: I like my room the most because

im3.text: Sure. I live in a three-bedroom apartment with my parents and my younger sister. It's in a quiet neighborhood, and there's a small park right in front of our building. The apartment is about fifteen years old, but my parents remodeled it a few years ago, so it looks pretty modern now. The living room has white walls, a long wooden table, and a big window that faces south, so it gets a lot of sunlight. To be honest, my favorite room is the kitchen. My mom loves cooking, and the kitchen always smells good. Whenever I come home tired, I go straight there and see what's for dinner. It always cheers me up.
phrases: To be honest, my favorite room is
so it gets a lot of sunlight

im3.text: Let me describe my place. I live by myself in a one-bedroom apartment that I moved into about a year ago. It's not huge, but the layout is really practical. The front door opens into a small kitchen, and then there's a living room with a sofa, a TV, and a bookshelf full of novels. My bedroom is in the back, and it's the quietest part of the apartment. I'd say my favorite spot is the living room, though, because I spend most of my free time there. I recently bought a soft rug and some warm lamps, and now it feels really cozy, especially in the winter. I love it there.
phrases: I'd say my favorite spot is

ih.text: Sure. I share a fairly old apartment with two friends from college. It's on the third floor of a red brick building, and honestly, the outside doesn't look very impressive. Inside, though, it's much nicer than you'd expect. When you open the door, you walk right into an open living room and kitchen area, which is where we spend most of our time. There are three bedrooms down a short hallway, and we each have our own, which is really important for keeping the peace. My favorite room is definitely the living room. We put a big wooden table in the middle, and on Friday nights we cook something together, play board games, and just catch up. Even though the building is old and the heating isn't great, that table makes the whole place feel warm. I honestly can't imagine living anywhere else right now.
phrases: it's much nicer than you'd expect
which is where we spend most of our time

ih.text: Okay, so I live in a house on the edge of the city with my wife and our two kids. It's a two-story house with a small yard, which was the main reason we bought it, because we wanted the kids to have a place to play outside. On the first floor, there's a big kitchen that opens into the living room, and on the second floor, there are three bedrooms and a study. The study is my favorite room by far. It's small and a little messy, but it has a big desk by the window, and I can see the trees in our yard while I work. After the kids go to bed, I usually go up there, make a cup of tea, and either read or catch up on work. It's the only quiet place in the house, so I really value it.
phrases: The study is my favorite room by far
After the kids go to bed

al.text: Sure, I'd love to. I live alone in a studio apartment in a fairly busy part of the city, so it's a bit noisy at night, but the location is perfect for my commute. The apartment itself is a single open space, maybe twenty-five square meters, with a kitchen along one wall, a bed tucked into a corner, and a small desk by the window. When I first moved in, it felt cramped, and I honestly wondered whether I'd made a mistake. Over time, though, I figured out how to make the most of the space. I put up shelves almost to the ceiling, I bought a folding table, and I hung a curtain that separates the bed from the rest of the room. If I had to pick a favorite spot, it would be the window seat I made with a few cushions. On rainy days, I sit there with a book and a cup of coffee and watch people rushing by on the street below. It's not a big home, but it really reflects who I am, and I think that's what makes it special.
phrases: the location is perfect for my commute
make the most of the space
If I had to pick a favorite spot

al.text: Of course. I live with my parents in an apartment that we've had for almost twenty years, so it's full of memories. It's a fairly standard layout, with three bedrooms, two bathrooms, a kitchen, and a living room, but what makes it special to me is how it has changed along with our family. For example, my old bedroom used to be covered in posters, but after I started working, I repainted the walls a soft green and turned it into something closer to a small office. My favorite room, though, is the living room. My parents have filled it with plants over the years, so it almost feels like a little indoor garden. In the evenings, my dad waters them while my mom and I talk about our day, and the whole room smells fresh and green. I know I'll probably move out in a couple of years, and to be honest, I think the thing I'll miss most is sitting in that living room with my family after a long day.
phrases: what makes it special to me is
the thing I'll miss most is

questions.tip_ko: 집 전체 → 방 구성 → 가장 좋아하는 방 → 그 이유 순서로 말해요. 좋아하는 방에서 실제로 하는 일을 하나 덧붙이면 답이 길어져요.

questions.question: Tell me about the things you usually do at home on a typical weekday. What do you do in the morning and in the evening? Who are the household chores shared with, and how do you divide them?

il.text: I wake up at seven. I eat breakfast in the kitchen. Then I go to work. In the evening, I cook dinner. I wash the dishes. I watch TV in the living room. I go to bed at eleven.
At home, I clean my room every day. My mom cooks. My dad washes the dishes. I take out the trash. At night, I read a book. Then I sleep. It is a normal day.

im1.text: On weekdays, I wake up at six thirty and take a shower. Then I make a quick breakfast, usually toast and coffee. I leave home at seven thirty. When I come back in the evening, I cook a simple dinner and watch a drama. I live with my sister, so we share the chores. She does the laundry, and I clean the bathroom and the kitchen. We take out the trash together on Wednesdays.

I live with two roommates, so we have a chore schedule on the fridge. This week, I am in charge of cleaning the kitchen. In the morning, I don't have much time, so I just eat cereal and go to school. In the evening, I study in my room for two hours. After that, I wash the dishes and talk with my roommates in the living room. Before bed, I read the news on my phone.

im2.text: Well, my weekday routine is pretty simple. I usually wake up around seven, stretch for a few minutes, and make coffee.
