I think the change happened because I finally had the freedom to choose it myself, instead of being forced. Funnily enough, I've even started taking piano lessons again, and this time I'm actually enjoying them.
phrases: in a direction I never would have expected

al.text: If I compare my teenage self to who I am now, the biggest shift isn't so much the genres I like, but the way I relate to music in general. As a teenager, music was almost part of my identity. I listened mainly to punk rock, and I deliberately chose music that my parents and teachers disliked, because it made me feel independent and a little rebellious. I'd play the same few albums over and over, and I took it very personally if someone criticized my favorite band. Nowadays, my taste is much broader. I listen to soul, jazz, some classical, and still a bit of punk on the weekends, but none of it really defines me anymore. I think a couple of things led to this. Growing older made me less concerned about how others see me, so I don't need music to make a statement. Also, having access to almost any song through streaming made it easy to explore without any risk. If anything, I've become more of a listener than a fan. I appreciate a good song regardless of who made it or what genre it belongs to, and honestly, I think that's made music even more enjoyable for me.
phrases: the biggest shift isn't so much ~ but

al.text: Looking back, my taste in music has gone through a kind of full circle. As a teenager, I mainly listened to whatever was trending on the charts, mostly upbeat pop and dance songs. To be honest, I chose music based on what my friends were listening to, because I didn't want to feel left out at school. In my twenties, I went through a phase where I rejected pop completely and only listened to underground hip-hop and experimental music, partly because I wanted to feel different from everyone else. These days, though, I've come back to pop, but with a different attitude. I listen to it because I genuinely enjoy well-made melodies, not because I'm following anyone. I think what changed is that I became more confident in my own preferences. I no longer use music to fit in or to stand out. On top of that, my job is mentally exhausting, so I value music that's easy and fun. It's funny, because the teenager in me would probably think I'm boring now, but I feel like I finally listen to music for the right reasons.
phrases: has gone through a kind of full circle

questions.tip_ko: 10대 때 즐겨 들은 음악과 지금 듣는 음악을 짝지어 비교하고, 왜 바뀌었는지 이유를 한두 가지 붙여요.

questions.question: You indicated in the survey that you like going to parks. Tell me about a park you often visit. Where is it, and what does it look like? Please describe it in as much detail as you can.

il.text: I often go to a park near my home. It is not very big. There are many trees and a small pond. There is also a walking path. I like this park because it is quiet and clean.
My favorite park is in the center of my town. It has a big field and many benches. There is a playground for kids. In spring, there are a lot of flowers. It is very pretty.

im1.text: I usually go to a park that is about ten minutes from my apartment. It is a medium-sized park with a lot of tall trees. In the middle, there is a small lake, and some ducks live there. There is a long walking path around the lake, and there are benches everywhere. On the weekend, many families come with their kids. I like it because it is peaceful.
phrases: about ten minutes from my apartment

im1.text: The park I visit most is next to the river. It is very long and narrow. There is a bike path and a walking path along the river. There are also some sports areas, like basketball courts. At night, the lights are on, so it is safe. I go there two or three times a week. My family and I love walking there in the evening.
phrases: The park I visit most is

im2.text: Let me tell you about the park I go to most often. It's a neighborhood park about ten minutes from my apartment on foot. When you walk in, the first thing you see is a big grass field. People sit there and have picnics. On the left side, there's a small pond with ducks, and there's a walking path around it. There are also some exercise machines for older people. The best thing about this park is that it's never too crowded, so I can really relax there. I usually go there with my dog on Saturday mornings.
phrases: the first thing you see is
The best thing about this park is

im2.text: I often go to a riverside park in my city. It's quite big, and it stretches for several kilometers along the river. There's a bike lane and a separate walking path, so it's safe for everyone. Along the path, there are convenience stores, public restrooms, and lots of benches. In the evening, the bridges light up, and the view is really beautiful. That's why many couples go there for a walk. I think it's one of the best places in my city. On weekends, there are also many people riding bikes and flying kites. It is free, too.
phrases: I think it's one of the best

im3.text: The park I visit most often is a small neighborhood park right behind my apartment complex. It isn't famous or anything, but I really love it. As you enter, there's a wide open lawn where kids play soccer and people lie on blankets. Around the lawn, there's a walking path lined with cherry trees, so in April the whole park turns pink. On the far side, there's a little pond with a wooden bridge. What I like most is the atmosphere. It's calm, and I can hear birds instead of cars, which is rare in a big city. I've lived near it for five years, and I still find new spots to sit and relax every season.

I'd like to talk about the riverside park in my city, because I go there almost every week. It's a long park that runs along the river, so it feels very open. questions.question: I'd like to talk about recycling. How does recycling work where you live? Tell me where people put their recyclables, what items they separate, and any rules people need to follow.

il.text: I live in an apartment. There is a recycling area outside. People put plastic, cans, and paper there. There are many big boxes. We must wash the bottles first. I think it is easy.
In my town, we recycle every week. We use special bags for food waste. We put paper and plastic in different boxes. We take them out at night. The rules are strict.

im1.text: I live in a big apartment complex, and recycling is very organized here. There is a recycling area behind my building. It has different bins for plastic, glass, cans, paper, and vinyl. People can take their recyclables there on Wednesday and Sunday. We have to clean plastic containers and take off the labels from bottles. Food waste goes into a separate machine, and we pay by weight. At first it was confusing, but now it's easy.

I live in a small house, so recycling is a little different. We don't have a recycling room. Instead, we put our recyclables in clear bags in front of our house. The truck comes three times a week in the early morning. We put paper boxes together with a string. Food waste goes into a small yellow bin. If people don't follow the rules, they can get a fine. So everyone is careful.
phrases: If people don't follow the rules

im2.text: Recycling is a big part of daily life in my neighborhood. I live in an apartment, and there is a recycling station in the parking lot. It's open every Thursday from morning until night. People bring their recyclables and sort them into large bags and bins. There are separate places for plastic bottles, other plastic, cans, glass, paper, and styrofoam. There's also a security guard who checks that people are sorting correctly. If you put something in the wrong bin, he usually tells you nicely. For food waste, we have a machine that opens with a card, and it weighs the waste. I think the system works pretty well.
phrases: a big part of daily life

im2.text: Let me explain how recycling works where I live. I live in a villa, which is a small apartment building, so there is no big recycling area. Instead, each building has a few bins near the entrance. People put plastic, cans, and glass bottles in one bin and paper in another. General trash has to go into special bags that we buy at convenience stores. The trash truck comes every night except Saturday. The most important rule is to empty and rinse containers before throwing them away. Some people don't follow the rules, so the area sometimes gets messy, but most neighbors try their best.

im3.text: Where I live, recycling is taken really seriously, and the rules are quite detailed. I live in an apartment complex with about ten buildings, and each building has its own recycling area. Every Tuesday evening, residents bring down their recyclables, and the area quickly fills with people sorting things into different containers. There are separate spaces for clear plastic bottles, colored plastic, cans, glass, paper, cardboard, and even old clothes. We're supposed to remove labels from bottles, rinse out food containers, and flatten boxes. When I first moved here, I made a lot of mistakes, and an older neighbor kindly showed me what to do. Food waste is separate, and we use a card at the machine so that we pay for how much we throw away. Overall, it's a bit of work, but I think it helps people understand how much waste they produce.

Recycling in my area is pretty well organized, although it's not exactly the same everywhere in my city. I live in an older neighborhood with houses and small shops, so we don't have a big recycling center. Instead, we put our recyclables outside our gate on certain days. Plastic and cans go in transparent bags, so the workers can see what's inside, and paper has to be tied together. Large items, like furniture or old appliances, need a special sticker that you buy from the community center. I once forgot to buy one for an old chair, and it stayed outside my house for a week! Food waste goes into a small bin with a tag on it. I think the system is fair, because people who produce more waste pay more, and that encourages everyone to throw away less.
phrases: I think the system is fair

ih.text: Recycling where I live is quite systematic, and I think it's one of the things my neighborhood does really well. I live in a high-rise apartment complex, and every building has a recycling area on the ground floor that's open twenty-four hours a day. It's divided into clearly labeled sections for paper, cardboard, plastic bottles, other plastic containers, glass, cans, styrofoam, and vinyl. There are also signs with pictures showing exactly what belongs where, which is helpful for children and older residents. The rules are pretty strict. For example, plastic bottles should be rinsed, labels have to be removed, and caps should be separated. Food waste is collected in a separate machine that weighs it, and each household pays a monthly fee depending on the amount. A few times a year, the management office also sends out notices reminding people of the rules, especially after holidays, when there's a lot of packaging. Overall, I'd say the system is a bit demanding, but it makes people more aware of their waste.

Recycling where I live has changed quite a bit over the last few years, so I'll describe how it works now. I live in a mid-sized city, in a building with about twenty apartments. Instead of a recycling room, we have a row of colorful bins in the back yard, and each color is for a different material: blue for paper, yellow for plastic, green for glass, and gray for cans. Recently, the building added a separate bin just for clear plastic bottles, because they can be recycled into higher-quality materials. Every resident got a small guide when they moved in, and there's a bulletin board where the manager posts updates. The trucks come on Monday and Thursday mornings, so most people take their recycling out the night before. What I like about the system is that it's simple to follow. What I don't like is that some neighbors still ignore the rules, and then the manager has to sort everything again. Overall, though, I think people here are becoming more careful every year.

al.text: Recycling in my area is pretty thorough, and I'd say it reflects how seriously people here take waste reduction. I live in a large apartment complex on the outskirts of the city, and each building has a dedicated recycling area beside the parking garage. It's open all day, but most people go in the evening after work. Inside, there are more than ten different containers, each clearly labeled with pictures and short explanations. Paper and cardboard go in one section, cans and metal in another, and plastics are divided into several types, including transparent bottles, colored containers, and plastic film like snack wrappers. Glass bottles are separated by color as well. The basic rules are that everything should be empty, rinsed, and free of labels or tape. Food waste is handled completely separately, through card-operated machines that charge by weight, which honestly made me more conscious of how much food I was wasting. Every few months, the management office posts reminders and sometimes even shares photos of incorrectly sorted items, which is a bit embarrassing for whoever made the mistake. All in all, the system takes some effort, but I think it works because it's consistent, and people know exactly what's expected of them.

I'd describe the recycling system where I live as strict but surprisingly efficient once you get used to it. I live in a small residential neighborhood with mostly detached houses, so instead of a central recycling station, each household is responsible for putting its own recyclables out on the curb. The local office assigns specific days for each material. For example, plastic and cans go out on Mondays, paper on Wednesdays, and glass on Fridays. Everything has to be placed in transparent bags so the collectors can check the contents, and if something is sorted incorrectly, they simply leave the bag behind with a warning sticker on it. That happened to me once when I first moved here, and it was a little embarrassing to see the sticker on my bag in front of my neighbors. General waste has to go in official bags that are sold at local stores, and since the bags aren't cheap, people naturally try to recycle as much as possible to avoid buying more. There's also a monthly collection for large items and electronics, which you have to register for in advance. It sounds complicated, but after a few months, it became a habit, and now I barely think about it.
phrases: once you get used to it

questions.tip_ko: 장소 → 분리하는 품목 → 지켜야 할 규칙 순서로 말해요. separate, rinse, flatten 같은 동사를 미리 외워 두면 묘사가 쉬워져요.

questions.question: Tell me about how you usually recycle at home. What do you do with things like plastic, paper, and food waste, and when do you take them out?

il.text: I recycle every Sunday. I put plastic in a bag. I put paper in a box. I wash the bottles. My brother helps me. We take everything downstairs. It takes ten minutes.
I live with my parents. My mom sorts the trash in the kitchen. I take out the food waste every night. On Wednesday, I take out the recycling. It is my job. It is easy.

im1.text: I usually recycle once a week. In my kitchen, I have three small bins: one for plastic, one for paper, and one for cans. When I finish a drink, I rinse the bottle and take off the label. I fold the paper boxes to save space. On Sunday evening, I take everything to the recycling area in my apartment. Food waste is different. I take it out every two or three days, because it smells bad in summer.

My roommate and I share the recycling work. She takes care of paper and plastic, and I take care of food waste and glass. We have a big basket next to the refrigerator for recyclables. When the basket is full, we take it to the recycling area together, usually on Tuesday night. It's not hard, but sometimes we forget to wash the containers. Then we have to wash them in the recycling area, which is annoying.

im2.text: My recycling routine is pretty simple, but I try to do it carefully. In my kitchen, I keep a few bags under the sink, one for plastic, one for cans and glass, and one for paper. Whenever I finish something, like a yogurt cup or a juice bottle, I rinse it right away, so it doesn't smell. I also remove labels and flatten plastic bottles to save space. Every Thursday night, which is recycling day in my apartment, I carry everything downstairs and put each item in the right bin. Food waste goes in a separate container in my freezer, so it doesn't smell, and I take it out every weekend.

I live alone, so I don't produce a lot of trash, but I still have a routine. Most of my recyclables are delivery boxes and plastic containers from food delivery. After I eat, I wash the containers and leave them to dry on the counter. I also remove the tape and labels from the boxes, because the rules in my building say we have to. Usually on Saturday morning, I collect everything in a big shopping bag and take it to the recycling area. It takes about fifteen minutes. Recently, I've been trying to order less delivery food, because I realized how much plastic I was throwing away.

im3.text: Since I live with my family of four, we produce quite a lot of recyclables, so we have a clear routine. In our kitchen, we have a recycling cabinet with four drawers labeled plastic, paper, cans, and glass. My parents made the labels so that even my little brother could sort things correctly. Everyone is responsible for rinsing their own containers right after using them, which keeps the kitchen from smelling. On Monday and Thursday evenings, my brother and I take turns carrying everything down to the recycling area. Honestly, I used to complain about it a lot when I was younger, but now it's just a normal part of the week. Food waste is my mom's job, because she's the one who cooks most of the time. She keeps it in a small bin with a lid and empties it every morning before work.

I have to admit that my recycling routine wasn't very good until last year. I used to throw everything into one big bag and sort it at the recycling area, which took forever and made a mess. Then my friend showed me how she organizes her recycling at home, and I decided to copy her system. Now I have three stackable bins next to my door, so I sort items as soon as I'm done with them. I rinse containers right after using them, and I cut cardboard boxes into small pieces so they fit easily. Every Sunday evening, I take the bins downstairs, empty them, and wash them if they're dirty. The whole process takes less than ten minutes now. It's much more efficient, and I actually feel a little proud when I see how neatly everything is sorted.

ih.text: My recycling routine has become pretty automatic over the years, so let me walk you through it. First of all, I try to reduce the amount of waste before it even enters my home. For example, I bring my own bags to the supermarket and buy refills for things like shampoo and laundry detergent. Still, there's always some packaging, so I keep a small sorting station in my utility room with separate bins for plastic, paper, cans, and glass. Whenever I finish using something, I rinse it, remove any labels, and put it in the right bin straight away. That way, I never have a huge pile to deal with at the end of the week. Every Wednesday night, I take everything down to the recycling area, and I usually chat with my neighbors while we're sorting. As for food waste, I compost some of it in a small container on my balcony for my plants, and the rest goes into the food waste machine. It's a small effort, but it makes me feel like I'm doing my part.
phrases: let me walk you through it

ih.text: To be honest, my recycling routine changed a lot after I moved in with my partner last year, because she's much more careful about it than I was. Before, I used to throw almost everything into the general trash, and I only recycled bottles when I remembered. Now we have a whole system. Under the kitchen sink, there are four bins, and next to the front door, there's a box for cardboard. Every time we get a delivery, we remove the tape and labels and flatten the box right away. We also wash takeout containers immediately, because if you wait, the food dries and it's really hard to clean. On Sunday mornings, we take everything to the recycling station together, which has actually become a little weekly ritual for us, followed by coffee at a café nearby. I have to say, I've learned a lot from her. I've realized how much waste I used to produce without even thinking about it, and now I feel uncomfortable throwing a plastic bottle into the regular trash.
phrases: Every time we get a delivery

al.text: I'd say my recycling routine is fairly disciplined, partly because I live in a building with strict rules and partly because I've become more aware of environmental issues over the past few years. The routine actually starts at the store. I try to choose products with less packaging, and I always bring reusable bags and containers when I buy things like tofu or meat at the local market. At home, I've set up a small system in the corner of my kitchen with labeled bins for plastic, paper, glass, and cans. The key to making it work is doing things immediately. As soon as I finish a product, I rinse it, peel off the label, and drop it into the correct bin, so recycling never feels like a big chore. For plastics, I also separate clear bottles from other containers, since they're recycled differently. Twice a week, on Tuesday and Friday evenings, I take everything down to the recycling area. Food waste is the trickiest part, so I keep it in a sealed container in the freezer until collection day, which completely solves the smell problem in summer. It probably sounds like a lot of effort, but once it became a habit, it honestly takes no more than ten minutes a week.
phrases: The key to making it work is

al.text: My recycling routine is something I've gradually refined, mostly through trial and error, and I think it reflects the fact that I work from home and have a fairly flexible schedule. During the week, I collect recyclables in a large drawer next to the kitchen, which I've divided into sections with cardboard dividers. Paper and cardboard go in the back, plastics in the middle, and cans and glass in the front, since they're the heaviest. I'm pretty strict about cleaning things properly, because I once read that a single dirty container can ruin a whole batch of recyclable material, and that stuck with me. Every Saturday morning, I go through the drawer, double-check everything, and carry it to the recycling station on my way to the gym. I've also started paying attention to items that can't go into regular recycling, like batteries, light bulbs, and old electronics. I keep those in a separate box and drop them off at special collection points every couple of months. On top of that, I've cut down on disposable items as much as possible; for example, I carry a tumbler and use cloth towels instead of paper ones. Overall, my routine isn't perfect, but it's consistent, and that's what I think matters most.
phrases: that's what I think matters most

questions.tip_ko: 집에서 모으는 방법 → 씻고 나누는 과정 → 내놓는 요일 순서로 말해요. usually, every, as soon as로 습관이라는 걸 드러내요.

questions.question: Have you ever had a problem or a memorable moment related to recycling? Maybe you made a mistake or saw something that surprised you. Tell me what happened from beginning to end.

il.text: One day, I put a dirty bottle in the recycling bin. The security guard saw it. He told me to wash it. I was embarrassed. I went home and washed it. Now I always wash bottles.
Last year, I joined a clean-up event at the beach. We picked up a lot of plastic. There were many bottles and bags. I was surprised. After that, I used less plastic.

im1.text: I remember my first time recycling alone. I moved into a new apartment last year. I didn't know the rules, so I put everything in one bag. The next day, the bag was back in front of my door with a note. It said I had to sort the items. I was really embarrassed. I asked my neighbor about the rules, and she explained everything kindly. Now I sort everything correctly.

When I was in high school, our school had a recycling competition. Each class collected cans and paper for one month. My class worked very hard. We even asked our parents to bring old newspapers. In the end, we won first place, and we got pizza as a prize. It was really fun, and I learned that recycling can be fun too.
phrases: When I was in high school

im2.text: I have a funny memory about recycling from when I was living in Japan as an exchange student. The rules there were very different from the rules in Korea, and I didn't understand them well at first. One week, I put my plastic bottles out on the wrong day. The next morning, they were still there with a big yellow sticker on the bag. My neighbor, an old lady, saw me and kindly explained the schedule with a paper calendar. She even drew pictures for me. After that, we said hello every morning. So my mistake actually helped me make a new friend.
phrases: I have a funny memory about

im2.text: A memorable experience was when I volunteered at a recycling center last summer. My university club organized it, and I thought it would be easy. But when I got there, I was shocked by the amount of trash. We had to separate items on a moving belt for four hours. Many things were dirty or in the wrong place, like food mixed with plastic. It was hot and smelly, and I was exhausted. But after that day, I started to wash and sort my recyclables much more carefully, because I know how hard the workers' job is.

im3.text: I'd like to talk about a time I made a pretty embarrassing mistake with recycling. A couple of years ago, I cleaned out my closet and found a lot of old clothes and shoes. I thought it would be fine to put them in the recycling area with the other items, so I left a huge bag there late at night. The next day, the building manager posted a notice in the elevator that said someone had thrown away clothes in the wrong place, and he included a photo of my bag! Nobody knew it was mine, but I felt so guilty that I went down and took it back. Then I found out there was a special clothing collection box near the subway station. I took everything there that weekend. Since then, I always check the rules before throwing away anything unusual.

One of my most memorable experiences with recycling happened when I took part in a zero-waste challenge with my coworkers last year. For one month, we tried not to produce any trash at all. At first, I thought it would be easy, but on the very first day, I realized almost everything I bought came in plastic. My lunch, my coffee, even the snacks in the office. I had to completely change my habits. I started bringing my own lunch box and tumbler, and I bought vegetables at a traditional market where I could use my own bags. By the end of the month, I had reduced my trash by more than half. I didn't completely succeed, but the challenge really opened my eyes, and I still keep some of those habits today.
phrases: By the end of the month

ih.text: The experience that comes to mind happened a few years ago when I organized a recycling campaign at my company. Our office had a big problem with waste. Every day, people threw away dozens of disposable cups and delivery containers, and nobody really sorted anything. I suggested to my manager that we try to improve the situation, and she asked me to lead the project. First, I set up proper recycling bins on every floor with clear signs. Then I made a short presentation explaining why sorting matters and what happens to waste that isn't recycled properly. At first, people weren't very interested, and some even complained that it was too much trouble. So I added a fun element: each team got points for correct recycling, and the winning team got a free lunch at the end of the month. Surprisingly, that made a huge difference. Within two months, the amount of general trash dropped noticeably, and people started bringing their own mugs. It was rewarding to see how a small idea could change people's habits.
phrases: The experience that comes to mind

ih.text: Something I'll never forget happened during a family trip to a small island a few summers ago. On our second day, we went to a beautiful beach that we'd seen in travel photos, but when we got there, we were shocked to see how much plastic was on the sand. There were bottles, fishing nets, and even old shoes that had obviously washed in from the sea. My kids, who were eight and ten at the time, asked me why there was so much garbage, and honestly, I didn't know how to answer. Then a local woman walked by with a big bag and told us that a group of residents cleaned the beach every morning. My kids immediately wanted to help, so we joined them for about an hour. Afterward, the woman thanked us and gave the kids small shells as a gift. That day changed how my family thinks about plastic. Since then, we've tried to use fewer disposable products, and my kids are now the strictest recyclers in our house.

al.text: The experience that really changed my attitude toward recycling happened when I visited a waste processing facility on a school field trip with my students last year. I'm a middle school science teacher, and I thought it would be a useful lesson for the kids, but I ended up learning just as much as they did. The facility manager showed us how recyclables are sorted, partly by machines and partly by hand, and then he showed us a huge pile of items that couldn't be recycled. He explained that much of it was perfectly recyclable material that had been contaminated with food or sorted incorrectly, so it had to be burned or buried instead. Seeing that mountain of wasted material was honestly shocking. One of my students asked whether recycling at home was pointless, and the manager said something I still remember: recycling only works if people do it properly at the very beginning. When we got back to school, my students started a project to teach the rest of the school how to sort correctly, and they even made posters for the cafeteria. It was one of the most meaningful projects of my teaching career, and it made me much more careful with my own recycling as well.

I'd like to share a slightly frustrating but ultimately positive experience I had when I moved into my current apartment about three years ago. The previous tenant had left behind an enormous amount of stuff, including old furniture, broken electronics, and boxes full of papers and plastic containers. The landlord said it was my responsibility to get rid of it, which honestly annoyed me at first. I had no idea how to dispose of large items properly, so I spent an entire weekend researching the rules. It turned out that furniture needed special stickers from the local office, electronics could be picked up for free if I booked in advance, and the rest had to be carefully sorted. I made several trips to the recycling area, and at one point, a neighbor who'd been watching me came over and offered to help. We ended up talking for an hour, and she later became one of my closest friends in the neighborhood. Looking back, what started as a stressful chore turned into a valuable experience. Not only did I learn the recycling system inside and out, but I also realized how much waste a single household can accumulate without anyone noticing.

questions.tip_ko: 실수했던 일이나 놀랐던 일을 하나 골라 처음부터 끝까지 과거형으로 말해요. 끝에 그 뒤로 바뀐 습관을 한 문장 덧붙여요.

questions.question: How has recycling changed compared to when you were younger? Describe how people dealt with trash in the past and what is different now.

il.text: In the past, people did not recycle much. They put all trash in one bag. Now, we sort plastic, paper, and cans. It is more work. But it is good for the earth.
When I was young, we used a lot of plastic bags. Stores gave them for free. Now, stores do not give free bags. I bring my own bag. I think it is better now.

im1.text: Recycling is very different now. When I was a child, my family didn't sort trash very carefully. We put most things in one big trash bag. Only newspapers were collected separately. Now, there are many rules. We have to separate plastic, cans, glass, paper, and food waste. We also have to wash containers. It takes more time, but I think it is better for the environment. People are more careful now than before.

When I was in elementary school, many things were disposable. We used paper cups and plastic spoons all the time. Cafés gave plastic cups even when people drank inside. These days, things have changed. Many cafés use real cups for customers who stay inside, and some people bring their own tumblers. Also, supermarkets don't give free plastic bags anymore. I think people care more about the environment now.

im2.text: I think recycling has changed a lot since I was younger. When I was a child in the nineties, my parents threw almost everything into one trash bag, and nobody really checked. We only separated newspapers and glass bottles, because some people collected them for money. These days, the rules are much stricter. We have to sort plastic, glass, cans, paper, and food waste, and we even need to remove labels from bottles. At first, people complained, but now it's a normal part of life. I think the biggest change is in people's attitudes. Young people today really care about the environment, and that makes me hopeful.

Compared to the past, I think recycling has become more organized but also more complicated. When I was in middle school, we had only two bins in our apartment: one for general trash and one for recyclables. It was very simple. Now, my apartment has about ten different bins, and I sometimes have to check the signs carefully. Another big change is food waste. In the past, we threw it away with other trash, but now it has to be separated and we pay by weight. Overall, I think the changes are good, because the amount of trash has gone down, even if it takes more effort.

im3.text: Looking back, I'm surprised by how much recycling has changed in my lifetime. When I was a little kid, my grandmother used to burn some of our trash in the backyard of her house in the countryside. Nobody thought it was strange back then. In the city, we had general trash bags and maybe a box for paper, but there weren't many rules. Now, the system is very detailed. We separate plastic, cans, glass, paper, styrofoam, vinyl, and food waste, and there are even special collection points for batteries and old clothes. Technology has also changed things. For example, my apartment has a machine that weighs food waste and charges us by the amount. I think these changes are definitely positive. They force people to think about how much they throw away, and I've noticed that I buy less unnecessary stuff because of it.

The biggest difference I've noticed is how much attention people pay to plastic now. When I was in high school, nobody really worried about plastic. We bought bottled water every day, used plastic straws without thinking, and got free plastic bags at every store. Nowadays, it's completely different. Many cafés have switched to paper straws, supermarkets charge for bags, and a lot of my friends carry reusable bottles and tumblers. I've also seen more shops where you can refill things like shampoo and detergent with your own container. Of course, there's still a lot of plastic waste, especially from food delivery, which has increased a lot in recent years. So I'd say people's awareness has improved a lot, but our habits haven't completely caught up yet. Hopefully, that will change over the next few years.

ih.text: Recycling has changed dramatically compared to when I was growing up, both in terms of rules and people's attitudes. When I was a child in the late nineties, recycling was something people did only if they felt like it. My family had one big trash can, and my mom would occasionally put newspapers and bottles aside, mostly because an old man in our neighborhood collected them to sell. There wasn't much awareness about the environment, and using disposable products was just normal. Nowadays, the situation is completely different. The rules are detailed and strictly enforced, and if you don't follow them, your trash might not even get collected. People's mindset has changed too. Many of my friends try to avoid single-use plastics, choose products with less packaging, and even shop at zero-waste stores. On the other hand, the amount of packaging has exploded because of online shopping and food delivery. So in a way, we're recycling much better than before, but we're also producing far more waste, which makes me think recycling alone isn't enough.

When I compare recycling now to when I was younger, I'd say the biggest change is that it's become everyone's responsibility rather than something only certain people did. When I was in elementary school, recycling was mostly an activity we did at school on special days. Our teacher would ask us to bring old newspapers or milk cartons, and the class that collected the most got a prize. At home, though, my family didn't really sort anything. Today, recycling is a part of everyday life for almost everyone. My apartment building has a recycling station with more than ten categories, and even my seventy-year-old father carefully peels labels off bottles every week. There's also much more information available now. If I'm not sure where something goes, I can just look it up on my phone in a few seconds. One thing that hasn't changed, though, is that some people still don't take it seriously, and their mistakes create extra work for others. Overall, though, I think we've made huge progress compared to twenty years ago.

al.text: If I compare recycling today with what I remember from my childhood, the difference is quite striking, not only in the systems we use but also in how people think about waste. Growing up in the early two thousands, I remember that recycling was fairly basic. My family separated newspapers and bottles, but most other things, including food scraps and plastic packaging, went into the same trash bag. Honestly, we didn't think twice about it, and neither did most of our neighbors. Over the years, though, the rules became much more detailed, and I think that gradually changed people's habits. Today, sorting waste into a dozen categories feels completely normal, and there's a real social expectation to do it properly. Another big shift is that the conversation has moved beyond recycling to reducing waste in the first place. When I was young, nobody talked about reusable cups or refill stores, but now these things are mainstream, at least among people my age. That said, I think we still have a long way to go. Online shopping and food delivery have created a huge amount of new packaging, and much of it is difficult to recycle. So while our recycling habits have improved enormously, the overall amount of waste is still a serious challenge.

The way recycling has evolved over the years is actually something I find quite fascinating, because it shows how quickly social norms can change. When I was in elementary school, my family lived in a small town, and there wasn't really a formal recycling system. Most trash was collected all together, and I remember people sometimes burning paper and leaves in their yards, which would be unthinkable today. Disposable products were seen as convenient and even modern, so nobody felt guilty about using them. Fast forward to today, and everything looks different. Recycling is highly organized, with clear rules about what goes where, and people who ignore those rules can actually be fined. What's even more interesting is that attitudes have shifted, especially among younger people. My teenage niece, for instance, refuses to use plastic straws and lectures the whole family when we order too much takeout. When I was her age, I wouldn't have even known what she was talking about. Of course, the system isn't perfect. There are still questions about how much of what we sort actually gets recycled. But overall, I think the change in mindset over just one generation has been remarkable, and it gives me some hope for the future.

questions.tip_ko: when I was young과 these days로 과거와 지금을 나눠 말해요. 바뀐 규칙 하나와 바뀐 사람들의 태도 하나를 들면 충분해요.

questions.question: Many people are worried about the amount of plastic waste these days. What concerns do people around you have about this problem, and what do you think should be done about it?

il.text: Many people worry about plastic. We use too many plastic cups and bags. It is bad for the ocean. I think we should use less plastic. I use my own cup at cafés.
People order a lot of delivery food. It comes in many plastic boxes. That is a problem. I think restaurants should use paper boxes. We can also cook at home more.

im1.text: Many people around me are worried about plastic waste. These days, people order food delivery a lot, and every meal comes in many plastic containers. My friends say the ocean is full of plastic, and sea animals are in danger. I agree that it's a big problem. I think we should use less plastic in our daily lives. For example, I bring my own tumbler to cafés and use cloth shopping bags.

My parents are worried about plastic waste because there is so much packaging these days. When we buy one small thing online, it comes in a big box with a lot of plastic inside. I think companies should use less packaging. The government should also make stronger rules. And people like me should try to buy products with less plastic. Small changes can make a big difference.

im2.text: Plastic waste is a serious concern for a lot of people I know. My friends and I often talk about how much plastic we use every day without even thinking about it. For example, when I buy a coffee, I get a plastic cup, a lid, and a straw, and I throw them all away after ten minutes. Also, food delivery has become really popular, so the amount of plastic containers has increased a lot. In my opinion, both companies and individuals need to change. Companies should develop better packaging, and people like me should use reusable products as much as possible.

One concern that people around me have is that recycling doesn't actually solve the plastic problem. My cousin works at an environmental organization, and she told me that a lot of plastic can't be recycled because it's dirty or made of mixed materials. That surprised me, because I thought sorting my trash was enough. Now I think the most important thing is to use less plastic in the first place. For example, I try to buy fruit and vegetables without packaging and avoid ordering delivery food too often. I also think the government should encourage companies to use simpler, more recyclable packaging.

im3.text: These days, a lot of people around me are worried about plastic waste, and I think it's become a common topic of conversation. My mother, for example, always complains when we receive online orders, because even a small item comes wrapped in several layers of plastic. My friends who have children worry about microplastics, which are tiny pieces of plastic that can end up in our food and water. Personally, I think the problem is that plastic is just too convenient and cheap, so companies keep using it. In my opinion, we need changes at different levels. The government should make stricter rules about packaging, companies should look for alternatives like paper or reusable containers, and individuals should change their habits too. I've started carrying a tumbler and refusing straws, and although it's a small step, I feel better about it.

One issue I hear about a lot is the plastic waste from food delivery. Since the pandemic, many people in my city order delivery several times a week, and each order comes with plastic containers, plastic bags, and disposable spoons. My roommate and I realized that our recycling bin was full of delivery containers every week, and honestly, we felt a little guilty. Some restaurants now let customers choose not to receive disposable utensils, which I think is a good start. A few delivery services even offer reusable containers in some areas. In my opinion, these kinds of options should be much more common. At the same time, I think it's up to each of us to change our habits. Since we noticed the problem, we've been cooking at home more often, and we only order delivery once a week.
phrases: it's up to each of us

ih.text: Plastic waste is probably one of the environmental issues people around me talk about most, and I think there's good reason for that. Everywhere I look, there's plastic. Supermarkets wrap vegetables in plastic, online orders come with layers of bubble wrap, and many cafés still use disposable cups for takeout. A few of my friends have become really passionate about this issue. One of them even organizes beach clean-ups every month, and she says the amount of plastic they collect never seems to decrease. People also worry about what plastic does to our health, since tiny pieces can end up in the food chain. In my opinion, recycling alone won't solve this problem, because only part of the plastic we throw away actually gets recycled. I think the real solution is to produce less plastic in the first place. That means governments need to set stricter limits on packaging, and companies need to take responsibility for the waste their products create. As consumers, we can also make a difference by choosing products with less packaging and supporting businesses that make an effort.

The concern I hear most often is that individuals are doing their best to recycle, but large companies aren't doing enough. A lot of people in my generation feel a bit frustrated about this. We carefully wash our containers and carry reusable bags, but then we see huge amounts of packaging in stores and wonder whether our efforts really matter. I understand that feeling, and to some extent, I share it. For example, last month I ordered a single phone case online, and it arrived in a box three times its size, filled with plastic air bags. Situations like that make me think the biggest changes need to come from businesses and governments. That said, I don't think individual actions are meaningless. When enough consumers demand change, companies usually respond. I've noticed that some brands have started advertising eco-friendly packaging, which shows that customer pressure works. So in my opinion, we should keep doing our part while also pushing companies and policymakers to take bigger steps.

al.text: Plastic waste is a topic that comes up quite often among my friends and coworkers, and I think people's concerns have become more specific over the past few years. At first, most people were worried about the visible problem, like plastic bags floating in the ocean or bottles piling up on beaches. Now, many people are also concerned about less visible issues, such as microplastics in drinking water and seafood, and the fact that much of what we sort for recycling doesn't actually get recycled. A friend of mine who works in the environmental field explained that mixed or contaminated plastic is often burned instead, which honestly made me question how effective our current system is. In my view, the solution has to involve several layers. First, governments should set clear limits on unnecessary packaging and make producers responsible for collecting and recycling what they sell. Second, companies should invest in packaging that's genuinely recyclable or reusable, rather than just labeling things as eco-friendly for marketing purposes. And finally, consumers like me need to rethink our convenience-driven habits. I've started small, by carrying a reusable bottle and choosing stores with refill options, but I know it's not enough on its own. Real progress will only come when all three groups move in the same direction.

I think the biggest concern people have about plastic waste is that the problem feels too big for any one person to solve, and that sense of helplessness can actually make people give up. I've heard friends say things like, why should I bother recycling when companies produce millions of plastic bottles every day? I understand that frustration, but I strongly disagree with that conclusion. In my opinion, individual actions matter, not because one person can fix everything, but because they shape social norms and influence what businesses do. A good example is how quickly cafés in my neighborhood started offering discounts for people who bring their own cups once enough customers began doing it. That said, I also think we can't rely on individuals alone. The production of plastic needs to be reduced at the source, and that requires strong policies, such as limits on single-use packaging and incentives for companies that develop alternatives. Education is also important, especially for children, so that the next generation grows up seeing waste reduction as normal. Personally, I've tried to lead by example. I avoid single-use items whenever possible, and I talk about these issues with my family without being preachy. If everyone does a little and keeps pushing for systemic change, I genuinely believe the situation can improve.

phrases: I didn't want to waste it, so

ih.text: Sure. The most memorable vacation I've spent at home was during the winter holidays about two years ago. I had originally planned to travel to Jeju Island with my college friends, but two days before the trip, one of them got sick, and we decided to cancel everything. I was pretty upset at first, because I had been looking forward to it for months. So I thought, why not turn my home into a little vacation spot instead? I cleaned my whole room, bought some candles and nice snacks, and made a schedule just like a trip. In the mornings, I went to a sauna near my house, and in the afternoons I tried new recipes, like Japanese curry and cream pasta. On the last night, my friends came over, and we had a small party with the food I made. We laughed about the canceled trip and ended up staying up until three in the morning. Looking back, I think that vacation was even better than the trip we had planned, because it was so relaxing and personal.
phrases: I was pretty upset at first, because

ih.text: Well, one home vacation I'll never forget happened last August. That summer was extremely hot, and I was exhausted from work, so I took five days off and decided not to leave my apartment unless I really had to. On the first day, I slept for most of the afternoon and felt a little guilty. But on the second day, I came up with a fun idea. I decided to cook food from a different country every day, as if I were traveling around the world. I made Vietnamese spring rolls, Spanish paella, and even Mexican tacos from scratch. Some dishes turned out great, and some were a complete disaster, especially the paella, which was way too salty. In the evenings, I watched movies set in the same country I had cooked for. By the end of the week, I felt like I had actually been somewhere. It was creative, cheap, and really relaxing, and it made me realize that a good vacation is more about your mindset than the place.
phrases: I came up with a fun idea

al.text: Sure, one home vacation that really stands out for me happened about three years ago, right after I finished a very demanding project at work. For almost six months, I had been working late nearly every night, and by the end, I was completely burned out. My original plan was to fly to Vietnam, but when I sat down to book the tickets, I realized I didn't have the energy to pack, deal with airports, or plan anything at all. So I made a slightly unusual decision: I stayed home for ten days and did whatever my body wanted. For the first few days, I mostly slept and watched comfort movies. Then, slowly, I started to feel like myself again. I went on long walks along the river, started reading a novel I had abandoned years ago, and even called old friends I had lost touch with. One of them came over with homemade kimchi, and we talked for hours about how much our lives had changed. What made that vacation memorable wasn't any single event. It was the feeling of finally slowing down. Since then, I've been much better at noticing when I need a break, which I think is a lesson I needed to learn.
phrases: I made a slightly unusual decision
What made that vacation memorable wasn't

al.text: Well, the home vacation I remember most clearly was during the Lunar New Year holiday a couple of years ago. Normally, my whole family travels to my grandparents' house, which means spending hours stuck in traffic. That year, though, my grandparents decided to come to our apartment instead, and for the first time, we hosted everyone at home. At first, I wasn't thrilled, because it meant a lot of cleaning and cooking. My mom gave everyone a job, and mine was making the dumplings, which turned out to be much harder than I expected. My first few looked terrible, and my cousins teased me about it all afternoon. But by the evening, my grandmother sat next to me and showed me her way of folding them, and I finally got it right. That night, we all ate together, played traditional games, and my grandfather told stories about his childhood that I had never heard before. I didn't go anywhere, and yet it felt like a real holiday. If anything, being at home made it feel more personal, and those stories are something I'm really glad I got to hear.
phrases: At first, I wasn't thrilled, because

questions.tip_ko: 과거 경험은 언제 → 무슨 일 → 어떻게 끝났는지 → 느낀 점 순서로 말해요. 과거형을 끝까지 지키는 게 중요해요.

questions.question: Compare the way you spend your vacations now with the way you spent them when you were younger. What has changed, and why do you think these changes happened?

il.text: When I was young, I traveled a lot with my family. We went to the beach. Now I stay home on vacation. I am tired from work. I want to rest. So now I like home more.
In the past, I went out with friends on vacation. We played outside all day. Now I am busy. I stay home and sleep. I watch movies. It is different now, but I like it.

im1.text: When I was a child, my family went camping every summer vacation. We went to the mountains or the beach, and it was very exciting. But now I usually stay home on my vacations. I work every day, so I feel tired, and I just want to rest. Also, traveling is expensive these days. So I think my vacations changed because my life changed. I miss camping sometimes, but I like relaxing at home too.

In my high school days, my vacations were very busy. I went to academies, and I studied almost every day. I didn't have time to rest. Now, I am a university student, and my vacations are much more free. I can sleep late and watch movies at home. I think it changed because I don't have big exams now. I like my vacations now much better.

im2.text: My vacations have changed a lot over the years. When I was in elementary school, my parents always planned family trips. We drove to the beach or visited my grandparents in the countryside, and the car was always full of snacks and noise. These days, I usually spend my vacations at home. I have a full-time job now, so when I get a few days off, I just want to rest and sleep. Another reason is money. Traveling has become really expensive, so staying home feels smarter. I sometimes miss those noisy family trips, but I also enjoy the quiet time I have now.
phrases: When I was in elementary school

im2.text: Well, when I was younger, I thought a vacation meant going somewhere far away. In my twenties, I traveled abroad almost every year with my friends, and we tried to see as many places as possible. But now, I prefer simple vacations at home. One reason is that I get tired more easily than before. Another reason is that I live alone now, so my home finally feels like my own space. I can decorate it, cook what I want, and rest without any schedule. I think getting older changed what I want from a vacation. Now I care more about rest than adventure.

im3.text: When I compare my vacations now with my vacations as a kid, the difference is huge. Back then, my parents planned everything. Every summer, we went to the same beach town, stayed in a small guesthouse, and spent all day swimming and eating watermelon. I loved it, but I never had any choice. Now, as an adult, I usually stay home on my vacations. I think there are two main reasons. First, my job is really stressful, so I need real rest, not a busy schedule. Second, I enjoy my own space more than I used to. I have hobbies I can do at home, like baking and drawing. Of course, I still travel sometimes, but home vacations have become my favorite.
phrases: I think there are two main reasons

im3.text: Well, the way I spend my vacations has changed quite a bit. When I was a teenager, I always wanted to be outside. I met my friends at the PC room, went to karaoke, or walked around downtown until late. Staying home felt boring. But these days, it's the opposite. I actually look forward to staying home during my time off. I think this change happened because my daily life is much busier now. I commute for almost two hours a day, so my home has become the place where I can finally relax. Also, home entertainment is much better than before. With streaming services and online games, I never get bored. So, I'd say my priorities shifted from fun to rest.
phrases: I think this change happened because

ih.text: Sure. If I compare my vacations now with the ones I had when I was younger, the biggest difference is that I've gone from always being on the move to really enjoying staying still. When I was in college, I spent every vacation traveling on a tight budget. I took overnight buses, stayed in cheap hostels, and tried to visit as many cities as possible. It was exciting, but honestly, I always came back more tired than before. These days, I'd much rather spend my vacation at home. I think there are a few reasons for this. First, my job is mentally exhausting, so I need time to truly rest. Second, I finally have a comfortable apartment that I've decorated the way I like, so being home feels like a treat. And lastly, I've just become more of a homebody as I've gotten older. I still travel once in a while, but now I see home vacations as a way to recharge rather than a second choice.
phrases: I think there are a few reasons for this

ih.text: Well, my vacations have changed a lot, mostly because my life situation has changed. When I was a kid, vacations meant visiting relatives. Every summer and every holiday, we drove to my grandparents' farm, and I spent the days running around with my cousins and catching insects. As a teenager, I spent most of my vacations at study academies, which honestly didn't feel like vacations at all. Now that I'm working, I finally have control over my own time off, and I've found that I prefer staying home. A big reason is that my weekdays are so packed that I rarely have a quiet moment. Another reason is that technology has made home vacations much more enjoyable. I can watch almost any movie, take online classes, or video chat with friends abroad. Of course, part of me misses the freedom of those childhood summers on the farm. But I think the way I spend my vacations now fits who I am today much better.
phrases: mostly because my life situation has changed

al.text: That's an interesting question, because my idea of a good vacation has really changed over the years. When I was growing up, vacations were all about going somewhere. My parents believed that we should see as much of the country as possible, so every summer we packed the car and drove to a different region, whether it was the east coast, the southern islands, or the mountains. Looking back, I'm grateful for those trips, but at the time I mostly remember being carsick and bored in traffic. In my twenties, I kept that habit and traveled abroad whenever I could, often with very packed itineraries. These days, though, I find myself choosing to stay home more and more. I think part of it is simply age. I value sleep and quiet in a way I never did before. But I also think it's about how stressful modern work has become. When you spend all week answering messages and attending meetings, the idea of rushing through airports doesn't sound relaxing at all. Staying home lets me slow down, cook properly, and spend time with the people close to me. So I'd say the change reflects a shift in what I need, rather than a loss of curiosity.
phrases: I think part of it is simply
rather than a loss of curiosity

al.text: Well, if I compare my vacations now with the ones I had as a student, they're almost completely different, and I think the reasons say a lot about how my life has changed. Back in high school, a vacation was never really a break, because I spent most of it at cram schools preparing for exams. Then in university, I swung the other way and tried to fill every vacation with something exciting, like backpacking trips, music festivals, or volunteering abroad. I was afraid of wasting my free time. Now that I've been working for several years, I've realized that resting is not the same as wasting time. So these days, I usually spend at least part of my vacation at home, and I plan it carefully. I'll set aside a few days to read, cook, and catch up with family, and maybe one or two days for a short trip nearby. I think the biggest reason for the change is that my energy is more limited than it used to be, and I've learned to protect it. Another reason is that I simply enjoy my home more now that I've made it comfortable. In a way, I feel like I've finally learned how to take a real vacation.
phrases: resting is not the same as wasting time

questions.tip_ko: 비교 문제는 예전 → 지금 → 바뀐 이유 두 가지 순서로 정리해요. used to, these days처럼 시점을 알려 주는 표현을 꼭 넣어요.

questions.question: I'd like to ask you about the technology people use these days. What kinds of devices or online services do you use most often? Please describe them in as much detail as you can.

il.text: I use a smartphone and a laptop. I use my smartphone every day. I send messages to my friends. I also watch videos. My laptop is old, but it is okay. I use it for school work. I like my smartphone the most.

I have a smartphone, a tablet, and a computer. My smartphone is black and small. I use it for music and maps. My tablet is for reading. My computer is at home. I use it for work. Technology is very useful for me.

im1.text: The device I use most is my smartphone. I use it for almost everything. In the morning, I check the news and the weather. I also use it for messages, music, and online banking. At home, I have a laptop too. I use it when I write reports or watch movies, because the screen is bigger. I also have wireless earphones. They are really convenient when I take the subway. Without these devices, my life would be very hard.
phrases: The device I use most is

im1.text: I use a lot of technology at home and at work. At work, I use a desktop computer with two monitors. I write emails and make documents all day. At home, I mostly use my tablet. I watch dramas on it in bed. I also have a smart speaker in my living room. I ask it about the weather or play music. These devices make my life easier, but sometimes I use them too much.

im2.text: Well, I'd say I use technology all day long. The most important device for me is my smartphone. I use it to check my schedule, read the news, and talk with my friends and family. I also use it to pay for things, so I don't carry my wallet very often these days. Besides my phone, I have a laptop that I use for work and online classes. It's a little heavy, but it's fast and has a big screen. Lastly, I have a smartwatch. It counts my steps and shows my messages. Overall, these devices help me a lot in my daily life.
phrases: The most important device for me is

im2.text: Let me tell you about the technology I use most. First of all, there's my laptop. I'm a university student, so I use it every day for assignments, presentations, and video lectures. I bought it two years ago, and it still works well. Second, I use the internet a lot. I search for information, watch videos to learn new things, and shop online because it's cheaper. And of course, I use my phone for messaging and taking pictures. I think I can't live without the internet now. When the Wi-Fi stops working at home, I feel really frustrated.

im3.text: Okay, so the technology I use the most is definitely my smartphone, and I'd like to describe it a little. It's about two years old, and it has a large screen and a really good camera. I take a lot of pictures with it, especially when I travel or eat at a nice restaurant. I also use it for my bank account, my bus card, and even my ID at the gym, so it's like my whole life is inside this small device. Honestly, it makes me a little nervous sometimes. When I left it at a friend's house last month, I felt completely lost for a whole day. Apart from my phone, I use a laptop for work, but my phone is the one I really can't live without.

There are a few devices I use every day, but the most interesting one is probably the smart speaker in my kitchen. My sister gave it to me as a birthday present last year. At first, I didn't use it much because I thought it was a toy. But now I talk to it every morning. I ask it about the weather, set timers when I'm cooking, and play the radio while I'm getting ready for work. It's really handy when my hands are busy. Of course, I also have a smartphone and a laptop like everyone else. I use my phone for messages and my laptop for work. But if you ask me which device surprised me the most, I'd say the speaker.

ih.text: Sure. These days I'm surrounded by technology, but I'd like to focus on the two things I rely on most: my smartphone and my home Wi-Fi. My phone is basically my office, my wallet, and my entertainment center all in one. I use it to answer work emails on the subway, pay for my lunch, and watch short videos before I fall asleep. What I like most about it is the camera, because I've been learning photography as a hobby, and it takes surprisingly sharp pictures at night. As for the Wi-Fi, I upgraded my internet plan last year when I started working from home two days a week. Before that, my video calls kept freezing, which was really embarrassing in meetings. Now everything runs smoothly. To be honest, I sometimes feel I depend on these things a bit too much, but I can't imagine my daily routine without them anymore.

Well, I'm not really a tech person, but I still use quite a lot of technology every day. The first thing is my laptop, which I use for my job as an accountant. I spend most of the day working on spreadsheets, so I need a fast computer with a comfortable keyboard. My company gave me a new one this year, and it's much lighter than my old one, so I can easily bring it home. The second thing is my smartphone. I mainly use it for messaging and checking the news, but recently I've started using a language learning app to study Japanese for twenty minutes every day. I also have a fitness band that tracks how many hours I sleep. Interestingly, it showed me that I sleep less than I thought, so now I try to go to bed earlier. So even though I'm not an expert, technology really shapes my daily life.
phrases: I'm not really a tech person

al.text: That's an interesting question, because I think the technology I use says a lot about my lifestyle. The center of everything is my smartphone. It's not the newest model, but it does everything I need: I manage my calendar, pay bills, read e-books on the subway, and stay in touch with friends who live abroad. Then there's my laptop, which I use for freelance design work in the evenings. I chose a model with a high-quality display because colors matter a lot in my job, and honestly, it was the most expensive thing I bought last year. I also rely heavily on cloud storage. All my files are saved online automatically, so even if my laptop broke tomorrow, I wouldn't lose anything. That gives me real peace of mind. If I had to describe my relationship with technology in one word, I'd say practical. I'm not the kind of person who lines up for the latest gadget, but I'm happy to pay for tools that genuinely save me time or make my work better.

Let me start with the device that probably changed my life the most, which is my tablet. I bought it about three years ago when I started graduate school, mainly because I was tired of printing hundreds of pages of research papers. Now I read and take notes directly on the screen with a digital pen, and all my notes are organized by subject, so I can find anything in seconds. It's honestly made me a much more organized student. Other than that, I use my smartphone constantly, like most people, and I have a pair of noise-cancelling headphones that I wear in the library. They block out almost all the background noise, which helps me concentrate for hours. At home, my family also uses a smart TV, and my parents, who used to be afraid of technology, now watch cooking shows and video-call my aunt overseas on it every weekend. Watching them enjoy it is actually one of my favorite things about technology. It shows how these tools can bring people closer, not just make work faster.

questions.tip_ko: 기기 두세 개를 정하고 각각 무엇에 쓰는지 하나씩 붙여요. 마지막에 내 생각 한 문장으로 마무리하면 답이 정리돼 보여요.

questions.question: Now tell me how you use technology on a typical day. When do you use your devices, and what do you mainly use them for, from the moment you wake up until you go to bed?

il.text: I use my phone every morning. I check messages first. On the bus, I listen to music. At work, I use a computer. At night, I watch videos on my phone in bed. I use my phone a lot every day.
I wake up with my phone alarm. I read the news on my phone. In the afternoon, I study with my laptop. In the evening, I play games. I go to bed at twelve. I put my phone next to my bed.

im1.text: My day starts with technology. My phone alarm wakes me up at seven, and the first thing I do is check my messages and the weather. On the subway, I usually listen to music or watch short videos. At the office, I use my computer all day for emails and documents. After work, I sometimes order food with my phone. Before I go to sleep, I watch a drama on my tablet for about an hour.
phrases: the first thing I do is

im1.text: I use technology from morning to night. In the morning, I listen to the radio on my smart speaker while I eat breakfast. Then I take online classes on my laptop because I'm a student. In the afternoon, I search for information for my homework. In the evening, I video-call my parents because they live in another city. I try to stop using my phone after eleven, but it's not easy.

im2.text: On a typical day, I use technology almost every hour. Right after I wake up, I check my phone for messages and look at my schedule for the day. While I'm commuting, I usually read news articles or listen to podcasts about economics, because I want to learn something on the way. At work, I'm in front of my computer for about eight hours. I write reports, join video meetings, and send a lot of emails. When I get home, I try to take a break from screens, but honestly, I usually end up watching videos on my phone until midnight. I know it's a bad habit.

Let me walk you through my usual day. I'm a university student, so my laptop is the center of my routine. In the morning, I check my class schedule and any announcements from my professors online. During the day, I take notes on my laptop in class and use the library's online database for my research. Between classes, I chat with my friends in group chats to plan our team projects. In the evening, I usually play online games with my high school friends for about an hour. It's the easiest way for us to keep in touch. Then I set my alarm and go to sleep.

im3.text: Well, my routine with technology is pretty regular. I wake up at around six thirty with my phone alarm, and before I even get out of bed, I check my messages and the news headlines. That's probably not a healthy habit, but it's hard to stop. During my commute, which takes about forty minutes, I usually study English with an app or listen to a podcast. At work, I use two monitors, and I have video meetings almost every afternoon, so my headset is always on my desk. After dinner, I try to do something without screens, like reading a paper book or going for a walk. But I have to admit, I usually pick up my phone again before bed and scroll through videos for a while. Lately, I've been trying to leave my phone in the living room at night.
phrases: before I even get out of bed

im3.text: Since I work from home three days a week, technology is a big part of my daily routine. On those days, I start working at nine by turning on my laptop and joining a short online meeting with my team. We use a shared calendar and a chat program, so I can talk to my coworkers anytime without calling them. Around lunchtime, I usually order groceries online, because it saves me a trip to the supermarket. In the afternoon, I focus on my projects and send files through cloud storage. When I finish work, I close my laptop and go to the gym, where I listen to music on my wireless earphones. At night, I sometimes watch a movie with my husband. Honestly, I can't remember how people worked from home before all these tools existed.

ih.text: Honestly, my whole day is organized around technology, from the moment I wake up until I fall asleep. My phone alarm goes off at six forty-five, and I immediately check my calendar to see what meetings I have. While I'm having breakfast, I listen to a news podcast on my smart speaker, which saves me from looking at a screen too early. On the subway, I use a language app to review Spanish vocabulary for about fifteen minutes, because I'm planning a trip to South America next year. At work, I'm a marketing manager, so I spend hours analyzing online data, editing presentations, and joining video calls with clients in other countries. After work, I try to set limits. For example, I turn on a focus mode on my phone at nine p.m., so only calls from my family come through. That small change has actually helped me sleep better. So while I use technology constantly, I've been trying to use it more deliberately.

My daily routine with technology is a little different from most people's, because I'm a nurse and I work night shifts. When I wake up in the early afternoon, the first thing I do is check my messages, since my friends usually text me while I'm sleeping. Then I check the hospital's online system to see my schedule and any updates about my patients. At the hospital, technology is everywhere. We use computers to record patient information, and the monitors beside each bed send alarms to our station if something changes. It can be stressful, but it really helps us respond quickly. During my break, I usually video-call my mom for a few minutes. When I get home in the morning, I put on a sleep mask and play white noise on my phone, which helps me fall asleep while it's bright outside. Without these small tools, working nights would be much harder.

al.text: My daily routine is pretty much built around technology, though I've become more careful about how I use it over the past year. I start the day at six thirty, and instead of grabbing my phone right away, I let my smart speaker read me the weather and my schedule while I make coffee. I made that change because I noticed that scrolling first thing in the morning made me anxious before the day had even started. During my commute, I usually listen to audiobooks; I've finished about twenty this year, which I never would have managed with paper books. At the office, I work in software development, so I'm basically coding, reviewing my colleagues' work, and attending online meetings all day. In the evening, I try to separate work and personal life by turning off work notifications at seven. Then I might cook with a recipe on my tablet or play an online board game with friends who live in different cities. Before bed, I put my phone on a charger in the kitchen, not in my bedroom. It sounds like a small thing, but it's made a real difference in how well I sleep.
phrases: It sounds like a small thing

al.text: If I describe a typical weekday, you'll see that technology shows up in almost every hour, sometimes in ways I don't even notice. I'm a high school teacher, so my mornings begin with checking the school's online platform for messages from students and parents. Some of them send questions late at night, so I try to answer before first period. In class, I use a digital board to show videos, maps, and student work, which makes lessons much more interactive than when I was a student. Between classes, I grade assignments online, and the system automatically calculates averages, which saves me a huge amount of time. After school, I usually go for a run with a smartwatch that tracks my pace and heart rate. I've become a little obsessed with improving my numbers, to be honest. In the evening, I relax by watching documentaries or reading the news on my tablet. The only time I really disconnect is on Sunday mornings, when I leave my phone at home and go hiking. I've realized that I need at least a few hours a week completely offline to feel rested.
phrases: The only time I really disconnect

questions.tip_ko: 아침 → 출근길 → 낮 → 저녁 → 잠들기 전처럼 시간 순서로 말하면 빠뜨리는 게 없어요. usually, after that 같은 연결어를 섞어요.

questions.question: Have you ever had a problem with a device or with the internet? Tell me what happened, how you dealt with it, and how the situation was finally resolved.

il.text: Last year, my phone broke. I dropped it on the street. The screen was broken. I could not call my mom. I went to a repair shop. It was expensive. Now I use a phone case.
One time, the internet stopped at my house. I could not do my homework. I was very worried. I called my brother. He fixed the router. It was okay after one hour.

im1.text: I remember a problem I had last winter. I was writing a long report on my laptop, and suddenly the screen turned black. I didn't save my file, so I was really scared. I called my friend who is good at computers. He came to my house and fixed it. Luckily, the program saved my file automatically, so I didn't lose everything. After that, I always save my work every ten minutes.

A few months ago, I lost my phone on the bus. I didn't notice it until I got home. I felt terrible because all my photos and contacts were in it. I used my laptop to find the location of my phone. It was at the bus station. The next morning, I went there and the staff gave it back to me. I was so happy. Since then, I always check my pocket when I get off the bus.

im2.text: I'd like to talk about a problem I had during an online job interview last year. I was really nervous, so I prepared for a long time. But about five minutes after the interview started, my internet connection suddenly stopped. I couldn't hear the interviewer, and the screen froze. I panicked and tried to reconnect, but it didn't work. So I quickly turned on the hotspot on my phone and joined the meeting again. I explained what happened and said sorry. Luckily, the interviewer was very kind and said it was no problem. I actually got the job. Now I always prepare a backup plan.
