One memorable problem happened when I was traveling in Jeju Island with my friends. We used my phone for everything, like maps, hotel information, and restaurant reservations. On the second day, my phone suddenly stopped charging. We were in the middle of the countryside, and we didn't know where to go. At first, we were really stressed. Then we went into a small store and asked the owner for help. She lent us her charger and even told us about a great restaurant nearby. In the end, it became one of our favorite memories of the trip. I learned that I shouldn't depend on one device too much.

im3.text: I had a really stressful experience with technology about two years ago. I was a senior in university, and I had to submit my graduation project online by midnight. Around ten p.m., when I was almost finished, my laptop suddenly made a strange noise and shut down. I tried to turn it on again, but it wouldn't start. I was so shocked that I almost cried. Fortunately, I remembered that I had saved an earlier version of my file in cloud storage that afternoon. I rushed to a twenty-four-hour internet café near my house, downloaded the file, and finished the last part as fast as I could. I submitted it at eleven fifty-five, just five minutes before the deadline. Since that night, I back up my files every single day, and I never wait until the last minute anymore.

Something funny but also embarrassing happened to me last spring. My company had an important video meeting with a new client, and I was the one presenting. I was working from home, and I thought I had turned off my camera while I was waiting for the meeting to start. So I was eating a sandwich and singing along to some music. Then my manager sent me a message that said my camera was on. I was so embarrassed that my face turned completely red. I quickly apologized, and luckily everyone just laughed. The client even said it made the meeting feel more relaxed. The presentation went well in the end, but now I always check my camera and microphone twice before every meeting. It was a good lesson, and my coworkers still joke about it.

ih.text: One experience I'll never forget happened when I was studying in Canada as an exchange student. About a week before my final exams, someone hacked into my email account. I found out because my friends started getting strange messages from me asking them to send money. At first, I didn't understand what was going on, and I felt really scared and embarrassed. I immediately changed my password, but the hacker had already changed my security settings, so I couldn't get back into my account. I went to the university's IT help desk, and a staff member spent almost two hours helping me recover it. She also showed me how to turn on two-step verification, which I had never heard of before. After that, I sent a message to all my contacts to explain what had happened. Thankfully, nobody had sent any money. Since then, I've been much more careful. I use different passwords for each account and never click on links in suspicious messages.

The most memorable problem I've had with technology was actually with my grandmother's phone, not mine. Last year, my family bought her a smartphone so she could video-call us. A few weeks later, she called me in a panic and said the phone was broken because the screen was showing everything in a foreign language. I drove to her house that weekend and found out that she had accidentally changed the language setting to Arabic. It took me almost half an hour to find the right menu, because I couldn't read anything on the screen. Finally, I changed it back to Korean, and she was so relieved that she made me a huge dinner. After that, I wrote a simple guide for her on paper with big letters, showing how to make calls, take pictures, and open her messages. Now she sends us photos of her garden almost every day. That experience made me realize how confusing technology can be for older people.

al.text: I'd like to tell you about a problem that turned into a pretty valuable lesson. A couple of years ago, I was in charge of organizing an online conference for my company, with about two hundred participants from five countries. We had tested everything the day before, and it all worked perfectly. But on the morning of the event, just ten minutes before it started, the video platform we were using went down for some reason, and nobody could log in. My phone started ringing nonstop, and I could feel my heart racing. I had to make a quick decision, so I set up a meeting on a different platform, sent the new link to all participants by email, and asked my coworkers to call the speakers personally. We started about twenty-five minutes late, which was embarrassing, but the conference went smoothly after that. Afterwards, several participants actually thanked us for handling it so calmly. Looking back, the biggest lesson was that you should always have a backup plan when you rely on technology. Now, whenever I organize an online event, I prepare a second platform and a contact list in advance.
phrases: I had to make a quick decision

al.text: The experience that comes to mind is a time when technology failed me at the worst possible moment. I was traveling alone in Europe a few years ago, and I'd planned my entire trip on my phone: train tickets, hotel bookings, maps, everything. On my third day, I was at a crowded train station in Italy when I realized my phone was gone. I don't know if someone stole it or if I dropped it, but either way, I suddenly had no tickets, no map, and no way to contact anyone. I remember standing there feeling completely helpless. Eventually, I calmed down and went to the ticket office, where a kind staff member let me use her computer to log into my email and print my train tickets. Then I bought a cheap phone at a nearby shop and spent the evening restoring my information from cloud backups. It cost me a whole day and quite a bit of money, but it taught me something important. Now I always carry printed copies of essential documents and keep a little emergency cash separate from my wallet. Ironically, losing my phone made me a much more confident traveler.

questions.tip_ko: 언제·어디서 → 무슨 문제 → 어떻게 해결 → 배운 점 순서로 말해요. 이야기 중간에 현재형으로 바뀌지 않게 과거형을 끝까지 지켜요.

questions.question: How has the technology people use changed compared to when you were a child? Describe what it was like back then and how things are different today.

il.text: When I was a child, we had a big computer at home. It was very slow. We did not have smartphones. Now, everyone has a smartphone. The internet is very fast now. I think now is better.
In the past, I called my friends with the home phone. I sent letters too. Now, I send messages on my phone. It is very fast and easy. But I miss letters sometimes.

im1.text: Technology has changed a lot since I was young. When I was in elementary school, my family had one desktop computer, and we shared it. The internet was slow, so it took a long time to download one song. Now, I have my own smartphone and laptop, and the internet is super fast. I can watch movies anytime. I think life is more convenient now, but people talk to each other less than before.

When I was a kid, I used to take pictures with a film camera. We had to wait a few days to see the photos. Also, I used a map book when we traveled by car. These days, I take pictures with my phone and see them right away. I also use a map app, so I never get lost. Technology made many things easier, but I think we are always busy now.

im2.text: Technology is very different now compared to when I was a child. Back then, my family had a heavy TV and a desktop computer that made a lot of noise. If someone used the phone, we couldn't use the internet at the same time, which was really annoying. To find information, I usually went to the library and read books. These days, everything is much faster and smaller. I carry a smartphone that is more powerful than our old computer, and I can find almost any information in a few seconds. I think the biggest change is that we're always connected now, for better or worse.

I think the biggest change is how people communicate. When I was in middle school, we used flip phones, and we could only send short text messages. Each message cost money, so we tried to write as few words as possible. If I wanted to talk to my friends for a long time, I had to call them on the home phone. Now, we use group chats, send photos and videos for free, and even have video calls with people in other countries. It's amazing, but sometimes I feel that conversations were more meaningful when we couldn't talk all the time.

im3.text: When I compare technology now with technology from my childhood, the change feels huge. I grew up in the nineties, and I remember that our family computer was in the living room, so everyone could see what I was doing. My parents only let me use it for one hour a day. To listen to music, I recorded songs from the radio onto cassette tapes, and I was so proud of my collection. Now, kids have their own tablets from a very young age, and they can watch or listen to almost anything in their own rooms. In some ways, it's great because they can learn a lot by themselves. But I also worry because parents can't really see what their children are doing online. Personally, I'm glad I grew up with fewer devices, but I wouldn't want to go back.
phrases: I wouldn't want to go back

im3.text: There's a big difference between the technology I used as a student and what students use today. When I was in high school, we wrote our reports by hand, and only a few students had laptops. If we needed information, we went to the library or used an encyclopedia at home. Our teachers used chalkboards, and sometimes they showed us videos on an old TV. Nowadays, my younger brother does everything on his tablet. He submits homework online, watches lectures on video, and even uses AI tools to check his grammar. On one hand, it's much more efficient, and he can study anywhere. On the other hand, I think he gets distracted more easily, because games and videos are always just one click away. So technology has made studying easier, but maybe not more focused.

ih.text: Technology today is almost unrecognizable compared to when I was a kid. When I was about ten, my family got our first internet connection. I still remember the strange noise the modem made when it connected, and how a single picture took almost a minute to load. We could only go online when nobody was using the home phone, so my mom and I used to argue about it. Back then, the computer was something you sat down to use for a specific purpose, like doing homework or playing a game. Today, technology isn't something we sit down to use anymore. It's with us all the time, in our pockets and on our wrists. I can pay for things, check my health, and talk to friends abroad without even thinking about it. Personally, I think the biggest change is not speed but how invisible technology has become. It's so built into our daily lives that we only notice it when it stops working.

When I compare the past and the present, I think shopping is where technology has changed the most for me. When I was a child, my mom and I used to go to the traditional market every weekend. We would walk from shop to shop, compare prices, and talk with the owners, who all knew our family. If something was sold out, we just had to come back another day. Now, I do almost all my shopping online. I can compare dozens of products in a few minutes, read reviews from other customers, and get things delivered to my door the next morning. It's incredibly convenient, especially because I work long hours. However, I sometimes miss the personal side of shopping. Nobody at an online store knows my name or asks how my mom is doing. So I'd say technology has made shopping faster and cheaper, but it has also made it a little lonelier.
phrases: When I compare the past and the present

al.text: If I think about how technology has changed since my childhood, the first thing that strikes me is how much more personal it has become. When I was growing up in the early two thousands, technology was something the whole family shared. We had one computer in the living room, one TV, and one landline phone, and we had to negotiate who got to use them and when. Those negotiations were annoying at the time, but looking back, they made us spend a lot of time together. Today, in my own family, everyone has their own phone, tablet, and laptop, and it's not unusual for the four of us to sit in the same room, each looking at a different screen. Of course, the benefits are enormous. My kids can video-chat with their grandparents in another city, and they can learn almost anything online. Still, I've noticed that I have to make a conscious effort to create shared moments, like a no-phone dinner rule. So while technology has given us far more freedom and convenience, I think it has also quietly changed the way families connect, and that's something we need to be thoughtful about.
phrases: the first thing that strikes me is

al.text: The difference between then and now is honestly enormous, and I think the change has been both exciting and a little overwhelming. When I was in elementary school, if I wanted to learn about something, say dinosaurs, I'd go to the school library, find a book, and maybe wait a week if someone else had borrowed it. Information was limited, but whatever I found, I trusted completely. Nowadays, the situation is the opposite. You can find a million pages about dinosaurs in a second, but you also have to figure out which of them are accurate. I see this with my nephew, who's twelve. He's incredibly quick at finding information, much quicker than I ever was, but he sometimes believes things just because they appear in a popular video. Another big change is that technology has become much easier to use. My grandparents, who never touched a computer, now send me voice messages and photos every week. So I'd say that technology has become far more powerful and accessible, but the skills we need have shifted from finding information to judging it carefully.
phrases: both exciting and a little overwhelming

questions.tip_ko: back then, these days처럼 과거와 지금을 나누는 표현으로 시작해요. 달라진 점 하나를 골라 예시와 함께 자세히 말해요.

questions.question: Some people worry that we depend too much on technology, for example by spending too many hours looking at screens. What concerns do people around you have about technology, and what is your opinion?

il.text: Many people use their phones too much. My friends look at their phones at dinner. I don't like it. I think we need to talk more. I try to use my phone less.
Some people worry about children and phones. Kids play games for many hours. It is bad for their eyes. I think parents should make rules. One or two hours a day is enough.

im1.text: People around me worry that we use our phones too much. For example, my mom always says I look at my phone even when we eat together. I think she is right. When I use my phone for a long time, my eyes hurt and I can't sleep well. So these days, I try not to use my phone after eleven at night. I think everyone needs some time without screens.

One big concern is personal information. Many websites ask for our phone number and address. My friend got a lot of spam calls after she shopped online. I think companies should protect our information better. Also, we need to be careful. I don't share my personal information on websites I don't know. I think technology is useful, but we should use it carefully.

im2.text: I think the biggest concern people around me have is that we depend too much on our smartphones. For example, my coworkers check their phones even during meetings, and my friends often look at their screens instead of talking to each other at cafés. Some people also worry about children, because many kids watch videos for hours every day. In my opinion, technology itself isn't the problem. The problem is how we use it. I think we should make simple rules, like no phones at the dinner table or turning off notifications at night. That way, we can enjoy technology without losing important time with people.

A lot of people I know are worried about privacy. Every time we use an app or a website, it collects information about us, like where we go and what we buy. My father, for example, refuses to use mobile banking because he thinks someone might steal his money. I understand his concerns, but I think it's impossible to avoid technology completely these days. Instead, we should learn how to protect ourselves. For instance, I use strong passwords and don't click on strange links. I also think companies and the government should have stricter rules to protect people's personal information.

im3.text: One issue that people around me talk about a lot is screen time, especially for young children. My sister has a five-year-old son, and she says it's really hard to keep him away from her tablet. If she gives it to him, he's quiet for hours, but if she takes it away, he gets really upset. A lot of parents feel the same way, and many of them worry that too much screen time can affect children's sleep and attention. Personally, I think tablets are not completely bad, because there are some good educational programs. But I believe parents need to set clear limits and spend time playing with their kids outside. In my opinion, the key is balance. Technology should be a tool for kids, not a babysitter.

These days, many people worry about fake news and false information online. For example, during a big storm last summer, my parents received a message saying that the subway would close for three days. They believed it and canceled all their plans, but it turned out to be completely false. Situations like this happen a lot, because anyone can post anything online, and false stories spread really fast. I think this is a serious problem, especially for older people and children, who might not be able to tell what's true. In my opinion, we should teach people how to check information, for example by looking at a few different news sources. I also think online platforms should do more to stop fake stories from spreading so quickly.
phrases: I think this is a serious problem

ih.text: One concern I hear all the time, both at work and from my friends, is that we've become addicted to our phones. Honestly, I think there's some truth to that. I once checked my screen time and found out I was using my phone for almost six hours a day, which shocked me. A lot of that time was spent scrolling through short videos that I don't even remember now. People also say it's affecting how we communicate. When I go to a restaurant, I often see whole families sitting together, each looking at their own phone without talking. Some of my coworkers also complain that they can't focus on long tasks anymore. In my opinion, the solution isn't to stop using technology, because it's too useful. Instead, we need to set personal rules. For example, I started leaving my phone in another room while I read, and I deleted some apps that I used too much. It's a small change, but I already feel calmer and more focused.

Recently, a lot of people around me have been worried about artificial intelligence. My friends who work in design and translation are especially concerned that AI might replace their jobs. One of them told me her company is already using AI to translate simple documents, so there's less work for human translators. Others worry that students will use AI to write their essays instead of learning how to think and write by themselves. I understand these concerns, and I think some jobs will definitely change. However, I'm not completely pessimistic. In my experience, AI is very good at simple tasks, but it still needs people to check its work and add creativity. I think the most important thing is to learn how to use these tools well, rather than being afraid of them. Schools and companies should also create clear guidelines, so that people use AI to support their work, not to replace their own thinking.

al.text: The issue that comes up most often among the people I know is privacy, and I think it's a much bigger problem than most of us realize. Almost every service we use collects data about us, such as our location, our shopping habits, and even how long we look at certain videos. Most of the time, we agree to this without reading the terms, because they're long and complicated. A friend of mine who works in IT once explained how much information a single app can gather, and honestly, it made me rethink a lot of my habits. On the other hand, I don't think the answer is to avoid technology altogether. That's simply not realistic, and these services do make our lives easier. In my view, the responsibility should be shared. Companies need to be more transparent about what they collect and why, and there should be strong rules with real penalties for misuse. At the same time, users like me need to be more careful, for example by checking app permissions and not sharing more than necessary. If both sides do their part, I think we can enjoy the benefits of technology without giving up our privacy completely.
phrases: If both sides do their part

al.text: There's an ongoing debate in my circle about whether technology is making us more isolated, and I find myself somewhere in the middle. On one side, people point out that we spend hours on social media but feel lonelier than ever. I've definitely experienced that myself. After scrolling through friends' vacation photos late at night, I sometimes feel worse rather than better, as if everyone else is living a more exciting life. My older relatives also complain that young people would rather text than call, and that real conversations are disappearing. On the other hand, technology has kept me connected with people in ways that weren't possible before. When I lived abroad for two years, weekly video calls with my family genuinely kept me going during difficult times. I also have an online book club with members from four different countries, and those discussions are some of the most meaningful conversations I have. So my opinion is that technology itself is neutral; it's how we use it that matters. If we use it to replace real relationships, it isolates us, but if we use it to support and extend them, it can bring us closer than ever.
phrases: it's how we use it that matters

questions.tip_ko: 사람들이 걱정하는 점 → 내 경험 → 내 의견 → 해결 방법 순서로 말해요. 장점도 한 문장 인정하면 높은 등급 답변에 가까워져요.

questions.question: You indicated in the survey that you enjoy walking or jogging. Where do you usually go to walk or jog? Describe that place for me in as much detail as you can.

il.text: I usually walk in a park near my home. The park is not big. There is a walking path and many trees. There are some benches too. I like this park because it is quiet. I go there in the evening.
I go jogging by the river. It is close to my apartment. There is a long path for walking and running. Many people exercise there. At night, there are lights, so it is safe. I really like it.

im1.text: I usually go walking at a small park near my apartment. It takes only five minutes to get there on foot. The park has a walking path around a pond, and there are lots of tall trees. There are also some benches and an outdoor exercise area. In the morning, many older people exercise there. I like this park because it is quiet and the air is fresh.

My favorite place for jogging is the path along the river in my neighborhood. It is about ten minutes from my house. The path is long and flat, so it is good for running. On one side there is the river, and on the other side there are flowers and grass. In the evening, the lights are on, so I feel safe. I go there almost every day.
phrases: My favorite place for jogging is

im2.text: Let me tell you about the place where I usually walk. It's a riverside park about ten minutes from my apartment. The park is long and narrow, and it follows the river for several kilometers. There's a walking path and a separate bike lane, so walkers and cyclists don't bump into each other. Along the path, there are benches, small playgrounds, and some convenience stores. In the evening, a lot of people come out to walk their dogs or jog. I like this place because I can see the water and feel the cool wind. That's why I go there whenever I need some fresh air.

The place I go jogging most often is a big park in the middle of my neighborhood. It's about a fifteen-minute walk from my home. In the center of the park, there's a large field, and a running track goes around it. The track is soft, so my knees don't hurt when I run. There are also tall trees, flower beds, and a small pond with fish. On weekends, families have picnics on the grass. I really like this park because it's clean and it never feels too crowded, even in the evening.
phrases: In the center of the park

im3.text: I usually walk along a trail on a small mountain behind my apartment complex. It's not a high mountain, so it only takes about forty minutes to get to the top and come back down. The trail starts right next to a bus stop, and at the beginning there are wooden stairs. After that, it becomes a dirt path with pine trees on both sides. Halfway up, there's a little rest area with benches and some exercise equipment. From the top, I can see my whole neighborhood, and at night the city lights look really beautiful. When I first moved here, I didn't even know this trail existed, but now it's my favorite place to clear my head after work.

My go-to place for jogging is the path along the Han River, which is about ten minutes from my place by bike. What I love about it is how wide and open it is. On one side you have the river, and on the other side there are big grassy areas where people set up tents and have picnics. The path is divided into a walking lane and a bike lane, so it feels pretty safe. There are also public restrooms, water fountains, and convenience stores every few kilometers. In the summer evenings, it gets really lively, with street musicians and people eating fried chicken on the grass. Honestly, jogging there never feels boring.
phrases: What I love about it is

ih.text: Sure, let me describe the place where I usually go walking. It's a lake park on the edge of my city, and it takes me about fifteen minutes to get there by bus. The lake is surrounded by a walking trail that's roughly three kilometers long, so one full lap is perfect for an evening walk. The trail is covered with a soft rubber surface, which is nice because it's easy on your knees. Along the way, there are willow trees, wooden decks where you can stand and look out over the water, and a small café near the entrance. What makes this place special for me is the atmosphere around sunset. The water turns orange, and you can hear birds everywhere. Even when I'm stressed out after a long day, walking around that lake calms me down almost right away. To be honest, I can't imagine living somewhere without a place like this nearby.

The place I jog most often is actually just my neighborhood, but there's a specific route I always follow. I start at the front gate of my apartment complex, go down a quiet street lined with cherry trees, and then join a stream-side path that runs through the middle of town. The stream itself is pretty narrow, but the city cleaned it up a few years ago, so now the water is clear and you can sometimes see ducks and even small fish. The path has stepping stones in a few spots, so you can cross to the other side. There are also outdoor exercise machines and little sitting areas under the bridges, where older people like to chat. I like this route because it's only about four kilometers, and it feels peaceful even though I'm in the middle of the city.
phrases: a specific route I always follow
even though I'm in the middle of the city

al.text: I'd love to tell you about it. The place I walk the most is a forest trail on a hill right behind my neighborhood. It's one of those places you'd never notice from the main road, but once you step onto the trail, it feels like you've left the city completely. The trail starts with a steep set of wooden stairs, which is honestly the hardest part, and then it levels out into a winding dirt path shaded by pine and oak trees. About halfway up, there's an open area with a few benches and some simple exercise equipment, and that's where most of the regulars stop to catch their breath. If you keep going, you reach a small lookout point where you can see the whole city spread out below you. On clear days, you can even see the mountains far in the distance. What I appreciate most is how the trail changes with the seasons. In spring it's full of flowers, in summer it's cool and shady, and in the fall the leaves turn bright red and yellow. It never really gets old.
phrases: one of those places you'd never notice

al.text: Well, the place I usually go jogging is the riverside park in my neighborhood, and I'd say it's one of the best things about living here. The park stretches for several kilometers along the river, and it has separate lanes for runners, walkers, and cyclists, so even when it's busy, you don't really have to worry about crashing into someone. The running lane is marked every hundred meters, which is great because I can keep track of my distance without using an app. Along the way there are big lawns, basketball courts, and a few outdoor stages where local bands sometimes perform on weekends. Personally, I prefer to go in the early morning, right around sunrise. At that time, the air is cool, the light on the water is beautiful, and the only people around are other runners, so there's this quiet sense that everyone is doing their own thing together. On the way home, I usually grab a coffee and sit on the steps by the water for a few minutes. By the time the park gets crowded, I'm already back home taking a shower.
phrases: one of the best things about living here
By the time the park gets crowded

questions.tip_ko: 장소를 위치 → 길과 시설 → 분위기 → 좋아하는 이유 순서로 말해요. bench, bike lane처럼 시설 이름을 두세 개 넣으면 묘사가 구체적이에요.

questions.question: Tell me about your usual routine when you go walking or jogging. What do you do before you start, while you are out, and after you finish? Please describe it step by step.

il.text: I walk after dinner. First, I put on my sneakers. Then I walk for about one hour. I listen to music. After that, I go home and take a shower. Then I drink some water.
I go jogging in the morning. Before jogging, I stretch for five minutes. Then I jog for thirty minutes. I don't take my phone. After jogging, I eat breakfast. I feel really good.

im1.text: I usually go walking three times a week after work. Before I leave, I change into comfortable clothes and put on my running shoes. I also bring a small bottle of water. When I start, I walk slowly for a few minutes, and then I walk faster. I usually listen to podcasts or music. I walk for about an hour. When I get home, I stretch a little and take a warm shower.

My jogging routine is very simple. I go jogging on Saturday and Sunday mornings. First, I drink a glass of water and do some stretching at home. Then I jog to the park near my house. I run about five kilometers. Sometimes I stop and rest on a bench. After jogging, I buy a cup of coffee and walk home slowly. Then I have a big breakfast at home.
phrases: My jogging routine is very simple

im2.text: Well, I have a pretty regular routine for walking. I usually go out around eight in the evening, after I finish dinner. Before I leave, I check the weather, and if it's cold, I wear a light jacket. I always bring my phone and wireless earphones because I like listening to music while I walk. First, I walk slowly for about ten minutes to warm up. After that, I walk quickly for about forty minutes. On my way back home, I sometimes stop at a convenience store to buy a drink. When I get home, I take a shower and stretch my legs. It really helps me sleep better.

I usually go jogging on weekday mornings before work. I wake up at six, drink a glass of water, and do some simple stretching for about five minutes. Then I put on my running clothes and go to the river path near my house. I don't run very fast. I just jog at a comfortable speed for about thirty minutes. I use a running app to check my distance and time. After I finish, I walk for a few minutes to cool down. Then I go home, take a quick shower, and eat a light breakfast like toast and a banana.

im3.text: My walking routine has become a big part of my day. I usually go out right after dinner, around seven thirty. Before I head out, I put on comfortable clothes and my favorite sneakers, and I fill a small bottle with water. I always choose a playlist or a podcast, because walking alone can get a little boring. For the first ten minutes, I walk slowly to warm up, and then I speed up and walk as fast as I can for about thirty minutes. If the weather is nice, I take a longer route along the stream. On my way home, I slow down again and stretch at a bench near my apartment. After that, I take a shower, and honestly, I feel so much lighter and more relaxed.
phrases: has become a big part of my day

im3.text: On weekends, I go jogging, and I try to follow the same routine every time. First, I check the weather on my phone the night before so I can decide what to wear. In the morning, I eat something small, like half a banana, because running on an empty stomach makes me dizzy. Then I do some stretching in front of my apartment building. I usually jog for about forty minutes, and I use a running app to record my pace. In the middle, I take a short break to drink water. When I'm done, I walk the last five minutes to cool down. Back home, I check my record on the app, and it feels great when I've improved a little.

ih.text: Let me walk you through my typical routine. I go jogging four times a week, usually early in the morning before work, because once the day starts, I never find the time. The night before, I lay out my running clothes and charge my earphones, so I don't have to think about anything when I wake up. In the morning, I drink a glass of water and spend about five minutes stretching, mainly my legs and lower back. Then I jog to the river, which takes about ten minutes, and run along the path for another thirty minutes. I usually run at an easy pace, but once a week I try to go faster to challenge myself. When I get back, I do a few more stretches in the parking lot, take a quick shower, and eat breakfast. By the time I get to the office, I feel much more awake than my coworkers.
phrases: By the time I get to the office

ih.text: My walking routine is pretty relaxed, but I stick to it most days. I usually head out after dinner, around eight, because walking right after eating helps with digestion. Before leaving, I put on comfortable shoes and grab a light jacket, since it can get chilly near the stream at night. I don't bring much, just my phone and keys. While I'm walking, I usually call my parents or a friend, so it doesn't feel like exercise at all. I walk for about an hour, and I try to reach at least eight thousand steps, which I check on my phone. On the way back, I sometimes pick up some fruit at a small market near my apartment. After I get home, I take a warm shower and stretch on the living room floor. It's a simple routine, but it really helps me unwind.
phrases: I stick to it most days
it doesn't feel like exercise at all

al.text: Honestly, my jogging routine is something I've built up slowly over the past couple of years, and now it's pretty much automatic. I run three or four mornings a week, usually around six thirty, before the streets get busy. The night before, I check the weather and set out my clothes, because if I have to look for my socks in the dark, I'll probably just go back to bed. When I wake up, I drink a full glass of water and do about ten minutes of dynamic stretching, things like leg swings and lunges, instead of just standing and stretching. Then I start with a slow jog for the first kilometer to let my body warm up. Most days, I run around six kilometers at a steady pace, but on Fridays I do short intervals, where I sprint for one minute and then jog for two. I always finish with a five-minute walk to cool down. After that, I record my run in an app, take a shower, and make a smoothie. I've found that having a fixed routine makes it much harder to skip a day.
phrases: instead of just standing and stretching

al.text: My walking routine is actually less about exercise and more about clearing my head, so it's pretty flexible. I usually go out in the evening, once I've finished work and had something light to eat. Before I leave, I change into comfortable clothes and put my phone on silent, because I really don't want work messages following me around. I don't use a fixed route. Some days I walk along the stream, and other days I wander through side streets I haven't explored yet, which is surprisingly fun. I typically walk for about an hour, and I try to keep a brisk pace for at least the middle thirty minutes so my heart rate goes up a bit. Every now and then, I stop at a small bakery or a bookstore on the way. When I get home, I stretch my legs, drink a big glass of water, and write a few lines in my journal about how the day went. That last part has become my favorite way to wrap up the day.
phrases: less about exercise and more about

questions.tip_ko: First, Then, After that 같은 순서 표현으로 하기 전 → 하는 동안 → 끝난 뒤를 나눠 말하면 길게 말해도 흐름이 흐트러지지 않아요.

questions.question: Think about a memorable experience you had while walking or jogging. When was it, where were you, and what happened? Tell me the whole story and why you still remember it.

il.text: Last summer, I went jogging in the rain. I did not have an umbrella. My clothes got very wet. But it was fun. I laughed a lot. Then I went home and took a hot shower.
One day, I walked in the park with my friend. We saw a small cat. It was very cute. We gave it some water. Then we walked again. It was a really happy day for me.

im1.text: I remember one day last fall. I went jogging along the river after work. Suddenly, it started to rain very hard. I didn't have an umbrella, so I ran under a bridge. Many other people were there too. We waited for about twenty minutes and talked to each other. When the rain stopped, I saw a beautiful rainbow over the river. I still remember it.

Last year, I joined a five-kilometer running event in my city. It was my first race. I was very nervous before the race. At the start, many people ran very fast, so I followed them. After two kilometers, I was very tired. But I didn't stop. I finished the race in thirty-five minutes. I was so proud of myself, and I got a medal.
phrases: I was so proud of myself

im2.text: I have a funny memory about walking. Last winter, I went for a walk at night in a park near my house. It had snowed a lot during the day, so everything was white. I was walking and listening to music, and I didn't see the ice on the path. Suddenly, I slipped and fell down in front of a group of high school students. I was so embarrassed, but they asked me if I was okay and helped me stand up. Luckily, I wasn't hurt. After that day, I always wear shoes with good grip in winter, and I walk much more carefully.

One memorable experience was when I got lost while jogging. A few months ago, I decided to try a new route in a different neighborhood. At first, everything was fine, but after about thirty minutes, I realized I didn't know where I was. My phone battery was almost dead, so I couldn't use the map. I asked an older man for directions, and he kindly showed me the way back to the main road. In the end, I jogged almost ten kilometers that day, which was twice my usual distance. I was exhausted, but it was a good lesson.

im3.text: The most memorable time I went jogging was during my first half marathon two years ago. I had trained for about three months, but on the day of the race, it was much hotter than I expected. For the first ten kilometers, I felt great, and I was actually running faster than my plan. But around the fifteen-kilometer mark, my legs started to cramp, and I had to walk for a while. Honestly, I almost gave up. Then a stranger running next to me said, let's finish this together. We ran the last five kilometers side by side, and I finished in about two hours and ten minutes. I never even learned his name, but I'll never forget him.

I'll never forget a walk I took with my grandfather when I was in high school. He lived in a small town in the countryside, and one evening he asked me to walk with him to the rice fields behind his house. At first, I didn't really want to go because I just wanted to play games on my phone. But as we walked, he started telling me stories about his childhood and how the town used to look. The sky turned pink and orange, and we could hear frogs everywhere. We walked for almost two hours without noticing the time. He passed away a few years later, so now that walk feels really special to me.

ih.text: Let me tell you about something that happened last spring. I was jogging along the river early in the morning, like I usually do, when I noticed an older woman sitting on a bench looking really pale. At first, I just ran past her, but something felt wrong, so I turned around and asked if she was okay. She told me she felt dizzy and couldn't remember the way home. I stayed with her, gave her my water, and called an ambulance. While we were waiting, I found her daughter's number in her bag and called her too. The ambulance arrived in about ten minutes, and it turned out her blood sugar was very low. A week later, her daughter contacted me to say thank you. Since then, I've tried to pay a little more attention to people around me, even when I'm focused on my run.

The most memorable walk I've ever taken was during a power outage in my neighborhood a couple of years ago. It was a hot summer night, and suddenly every light on the street went out. Since there was no air conditioning, a lot of people came outside, including me. I decided to walk to the park, and it was such a strange experience. Without the streetlights, I could actually see the stars, which almost never happens in the city. Neighbors I had never talked to were sitting outside, sharing snacks and chatting with each other. Some kids were running around with flashlights. The power came back about two hours later, and everything went back to normal pretty quickly. But I still remember how calm and friendly everything felt that night, and it made me realize how little I know the people living around me.

al.text: One run that really sticks with me is a night race I did along the Han River about three years ago. I had signed up mostly because a friend dragged me into it, and to be honest, I hadn't trained nearly as much as I should have. The race started at nine at night, and there were thousands of runners wearing glowing bracelets, so the whole riverside looked like a river of light. For the first few kilometers, I was having the time of my life, chatting with my friend and enjoying the view of the bridges lit up over the water. But around the seventh kilometer, I hit a wall. My legs felt like stone, and I seriously considered dropping out. My friend could have run ahead, but she slowed down and stayed with me the whole way, making jokes to keep me going. We crossed the finish line together, almost an hour slower than we had planned, but laughing the entire time. That night taught me that finishing something with someone can matter more than the time on the clock.

I'd have to say the most memorable walk I've had was the day I found out I'd gotten my first job. I had been waiting for the result for almost two weeks, and I was so anxious that I couldn't sit still at home, so I went out for a walk along the stream near my apartment. About twenty minutes into the walk, my phone buzzed, and it was an email from the company. I remember stopping in the middle of the path, too nervous to open it. When I finally read that I had been accepted, I actually shouted out loud, and a couple walking their dog turned around and stared at me. I was a little embarrassed, but I couldn't stop smiling. Instead of going home, I kept walking for another hour, calling my parents and my best friend one by one. My mom actually cried on the phone, which made me tear up a little too. Even now, whenever I walk past that particular bridge, I remember exactly how I felt in that moment.

questions.tip_ko: 언제·어디서를 먼저 말하고, 무슨 일이 있었는지 과거형으로 이어 가요. 마지막에 그 일로 느낀 점이나 바뀐 점을 한 문장 붙이면 마무리가 깔끔해요.

questions.question: How has the way you walk or jog changed since you first started? Compare how you used to do it with how you do it now, and explain what caused those changes.

il.text: Before, I walked only on weekends. Now I walk every day. Before, I walked alone. Now I walk with my sister. I like walking now more than before. It is good for my health.
When I started jogging, I ran only ten minutes. It was very hard. Now I run thirty minutes. It is easy now. Before, I had cheap shoes. Now I have good running shoes.

im1.text: When I first started jogging, I was really slow. I could only run for about ten minutes without stopping. I also didn't stretch, so my legs hurt a lot. Now, I can run for forty minutes, and I always stretch before and after running. In the past, I ran alone, but now I sometimes run with a running club on weekends. I think I enjoy jogging more now than before.

In the past, I walked only to go somewhere, like to the bus stop or to school. I didn't think it was exercise. But now I walk for my health. I walk for one hour almost every evening. I also check my steps on my phone. Before, I didn't care about my health, but now I care a lot because I sit at my desk all day.

im2.text: My jogging style has changed a lot since I started. Three years ago, when I first began, I just put on any old sneakers and ran as fast as I could. Because of that, I got tired very quickly, and my knees often hurt. These days, I'm much smarter about it. I bought proper running shoes, and I always warm up and cool down. I also run at a slower, steady pace, so I can run much longer than before. Another big change is that I used to run only when I felt like it, but now I have a regular schedule. I think the biggest reason for these changes is that I learned a lot from online videos.

When I was in college, I walked a lot, but only because I didn't have a car. I walked to class, to my part-time job, and to my friends' houses. It wasn't for exercise at all. Now I drive to work, so I don't walk much during the day. That's why I started taking walks in the evening on purpose. Another difference is that I used to walk quickly because I was always late, but now I walk slowly and enjoy the scenery. I think walking has changed from something I had to do into something I want to do.

im3.text: Compared to when I first started, the way I walk has changed quite a bit. A few years ago, I only went walking when I felt stressed, maybe once or twice a month. I didn't plan anything. I just walked around the block and came home. These days, walking is part of my daily schedule. I go out almost every evening, and I usually walk for about an hour along the stream. I also use a smartwatch to check my steps and heart rate, which I never did before. The main reason for this change was a health checkup two years ago. The doctor told me my blood pressure was a little high, and he said walking every day would help. Since then, I've taken it much more seriously.
phrases: Compared to when I first started
The main reason for this change

im3.text: My jogging habits are really different now compared to when I was younger. In my early twenties, I used to run with my friends late at night, and it was more of a social thing than exercise. We'd run for twenty minutes and then go eat chicken together, so I don't think it was very healthy. Now that I'm in my thirties, I jog alone in the early morning, and I focus on my breathing and my pace. I also pay attention to things like stretching and getting enough sleep. I think the biggest reason is that my body doesn't recover as quickly as before, so I have to be more careful. Still, I miss those fun late-night runs sometimes.
phrases: Now that I'm in my thirties
doesn't recover as quickly as before

ih.text: There's actually a big difference between how I used to walk and how I walk now. When I first started walking for exercise, about five years ago, I saw it as something boring that I had to do to lose weight. I'd walk the same short route every day, constantly checking the time and counting down the minutes until I could go home. These days, it's completely different. I walk because I genuinely enjoy it, and I often go much farther than I planned. I explore new neighborhoods, take photos of interesting buildings, and sometimes stop at small cafés along the way. I think the turning point was when I started listening to audiobooks while walking. Suddenly, the time flew by, and I actually looked forward to going out. Now, if I skip a day, I feel like something's missing.

When I first started jogging, I was honestly pretty bad at it. I'd run as fast as I could for the first few minutes and then end up walking, completely out of breath. I didn't have proper shoes, I never stretched, and after a couple of weeks I hurt my ankle and had to stop for a month. These days, I approach jogging in a much more careful way. I start slowly, keep a steady pace, and I increase my distance only a little each week. I also joined a small running group in my neighborhood, and the members taught me a lot about breathing and posture. The biggest change, though, is my mindset. In the past, I only cared about losing weight quickly, but now I care more about staying healthy for the long term, so I don't push myself too hard.

al.text: The way I jog now is almost unrecognizable compared to how I started. Back when I first got into it, I was a university student, and I'd basically go out whenever I felt guilty about eating too much. There was no plan at all. I'd run until I got tired, which usually didn't take very long, and then I'd walk home feeling a bit defeated. Over the years, though, things have changed quite a lot. I now follow a weekly plan with easy runs, one long run on the weekend, and a short session of faster intervals. I track everything with an app, and I've learned to listen to my body, so if my knees feel sore, I take a rest day instead of pushing through. Another big difference is the reason I run. In the past, it was mostly about appearance, but now it's about my mental health. After a stressful day at work, a run is the one thing that reliably clears my head. If I had to pick the main cause of this change, I'd say it was getting older and realizing that health isn't something you can take for granted.

If I compare how I walked when I was a kid with how I walk now, the difference is pretty huge, and I think it says a lot about how my neighborhood has changed too. When I was little, I walked everywhere, mostly because there was nothing else to do. My friends and I would wander around the alleys after school, stopping at small stationery shops and playing in empty lots until dinner time. Back then, walking was just part of life, not something you planned. Nowadays, I live in a big apartment complex, and most of my daily trips are by car or subway, so if I don't make an effort, I barely walk at all. That's why I now schedule walks the same way I'd schedule a meeting. I go out three or four evenings a week, and I try to choose routes with parks or streams rather than busy roads. In a way, I've had to rediscover walking as an adult. It's less spontaneous than it used to be, but I probably appreciate it more now than I did as a kid.

questions.tip_ko: used to로 예전 모습을, these days나 now로 지금 모습을 말해요. 바뀐 이유를 하나 꼭 넣어야 비교 문제의 답이 완성돼요.

questions.question: Let's talk about the weather in your country. What are the seasons like where you live? Describe the weather in each season in as much detail as possible.

il.text: Korea has four seasons. Spring is warm. Summer is very hot and rainy. Fall is cool and nice. Winter is cold and dry. Sometimes it snows. I like fall the most.
In Korea, there are four seasons. In spring, there are many flowers. In summer, it is hot and humid. In fall, the sky is blue. In winter, it is very cold. My favorite is spring.

im1.text: Korea has four clear seasons. Spring starts in March, and it's warm and sunny. There are cherry blossoms everywhere. Summer is really hot and humid, and we have a rainy season in July. Fall is my favorite season because the weather is cool and the leaves turn red and yellow. Winter is very cold and dry, and sometimes it snows a lot. Each season is different, so it's never boring.

Where I live, we have four seasons. In spring, the weather is mild, but sometimes there is a lot of fine dust. Summer is long and very hot. It rains a lot in July, too. In fall, the air is cool and fresh, so it's great for hiking. Winter is cold, and the wind is strong. I don't like winter much because I get cold easily. But I love the snow.

im2.text: Well, Korea has four distinct seasons, and each one feels very different. Spring comes in March and April. It's warm during the day but still chilly at night, and cherry blossoms are everywhere. Summer is hot and sticky, and there's a rainy season called jangma, usually in July. After that, fall arrives, and honestly, it's the best time of the year. The sky is clear and blue, and the mountains turn red and orange. Finally, winter is long and cold, especially in January, and it often snows. Because the seasons change so much, people here change their clothes and food with every season.
phrases: honestly, it's the best time of the year
Because the seasons change so much

im2.text: Sure. In my country, we have spring, summer, fall, and winter. Spring is short but beautiful, with lots of flowers, although yellow dust sometimes makes the sky gray. Summer is my least favorite season. It's extremely humid, and the temperature often goes over thirty degrees. Fall is cool and dry, so many people go hiking or have picnics. Winter is freezing, and the wind can be really strong. I always wear a long padded coat when I go out. Even though the weather can be extreme, I like having four seasons because there's always something to look forward to.
phrases: there's always something to look forward to

im3.text: Okay, so Korea is known for having four clear seasons, and I think each one has its own charm. Spring usually starts in late March. The weather gets warmer, and the streets are full of cherry blossoms and yellow forsythia, although we sometimes have fine dust, so people wear masks. Summer starts in June, and it gets really hot and humid. In July, we have the monsoon season, which means it rains almost every day for a few weeks. Then fall comes, and the weather becomes cool and dry. It's perfect for hiking because the mountains are covered in colorful leaves. Finally, winter is cold, windy, and dry. In January, the temperature often drops below minus ten degrees. Personally, I like fall the most, but I enjoy watching the seasons change.
phrases: each one has its own charm

im3.text: Well, where I live, the four seasons are very clear, and the weather changes a lot during the year. In spring, it's warm and pleasant, but the temperature changes a lot between morning and afternoon, so people often catch colds. Summer is the hardest season for me. It's not just hot, it's really humid, so you sweat even when you're just walking. There's also a rainy season in the middle of summer, and sometimes typhoons come in August. Fall is short but wonderful. The air is crisp, and the sky looks higher and bluer. Winter is long and cold, and when the wind blows from the north, it feels freezing. I've noticed that the seasons feel different than before, though. Spring and fall are getting shorter every year.

ih.text: Sure. Korea has four very distinct seasons, and honestly, the weather shapes a lot of our daily life. Spring begins around March. It's mild and sunny, and by early April, the cherry blossoms are in full bloom, so parks get really crowded. The downside is fine dust, which can make the sky look gray and hazy for days. Summer starts in June and gets more intense every week. By July, we're in the rainy season, and it can pour for days without stopping. Then August is just hot and sticky, and air conditioners run all day. Fall is my favorite season by far. From late September, the air becomes cool and dry, the sky is clear, and the mountains turn red and gold. Winter is the opposite of summer. It's dry and bitterly cold, especially when the wind comes from the north, and it often snows in January. What I find interesting is that each season has its own food, clothes, and activities, so the year always feels like it's changing.
phrases: the weather shapes a lot of our daily life
What I find interesting is that

ih.text: Well, the weather in Korea is pretty dramatic, because we have four clear seasons and big temperature differences between them. In spring, the weather is warm and gentle, and it's the season when everyone wants to go outside to see the flowers. However, the temperature can drop suddenly at night, so you always need a light jacket. Summer, on the other hand, is long and tough. It's hot, the humidity is really high, and in July we get the monsoon rains. Some years we also get typhoons, which bring strong winds and heavy rain. Fall is short, but it's probably the most comfortable season. It's cool and clear, and people go hiking to see the autumn leaves. Winter is dry and freezing, and the cold wind can feel painful on your face. Personally, I think the changes between seasons are what make life here interesting. But to be honest, I've noticed that summers are getting longer and hotter, and spring and fall seem to pass by faster than they used to.
phrases: the changes between seasons are what make
pass by faster than they used to

al.text: Sure, I'd love to talk about that. In Korea, we have four distinct seasons, and I think living here makes you very aware of how weather affects your mood and routine. Spring usually begins in March, and for a few weeks the whole country seems to come alive. The cherry blossoms bloom, people go on picnics, and cafés open their windows. That said, spring isn't perfect, because we often have fine dust that comes with the wind, so on some days you have to wear a mask and stay inside. Summer is a completely different story. It's hot and extremely humid, and in July we have the monsoon season, when it can rain heavily for weeks. By August, it's so sticky that most people just move from one air-conditioned place to another. Then, almost overnight, fall arrives. The air turns cool and crisp, the sky becomes incredibly clear, and the mountains are covered in red and yellow leaves. Honestly, it's the season I look forward to all year. Winter, finally, is long, dry, and bitterly cold, especially when the wind comes down from the north. Even so, I like how each season has its own food, festivals, and atmosphere.

Well, the weather where I live is defined by four clear seasons, and each one is so different that it almost feels like living in four different places during the year. Spring is mild and bright, and it's the time when everyone suddenly wants to be outdoors. Rivers and parks fill up with people taking photos of the flowers. The only real problem is the air quality, because there are days when fine dust turns the sky a dull yellow. Summer, by contrast, is intense. The temperature regularly goes above thirty degrees, the humidity is exhausting, and the monsoon in July brings days of heavy rain, sometimes with flooding in low areas. Fall is the reward for surviving summer. It's cool, dry, and sunny, and I think the autumn leaves in the mountains are one of the most beautiful sights in the country. Winter is harsh, with dry, freezing air and occasional heavy snow. One thing I've really noticed in recent years, though, is that the balance between the seasons is shifting. Summers seem to start earlier and last longer, while spring and fall feel shorter. It makes me a little worried about what the seasons will be like in the future.
phrases: One thing I've really noticed in recent years

questions.tip_ko: 계절 네 개를 순서대로 말하고, 계절마다 기온·하늘·하는 일 중 두 가지를 붙여요. 마지막에 좋아하는 계절 한 문장이면 충분해요.

questions.question: How does the weather affect what you do every day? Tell me about the things you usually do to prepare for the weather, for example in summer or winter.

il.text: I check the weather every morning. In summer, I wear a T-shirt. I carry an umbrella. In winter, I wear a long coat and gloves. I drink hot tea. I stay inside a lot.
The weather is important to me. When it rains, I take the bus. When it is sunny, I walk. In summer, I use a fan. In winter, I wear a hat. I check the app every day.
phrases: I check the app every day

im1.text: Every morning, I check the weather app on my phone before I get dressed. In summer, I wear light clothes and always carry a small umbrella because it rains suddenly. I also drink a lot of water. In winter, I wear a thick padded coat, a scarf, and gloves. I also check the fine dust level, and if it's bad, I wear a mask. The weather really changes my daily plans.

The weather changes my routine a lot. When it's hot in summer, I go to the gym in the early morning, not in the afternoon. I also bring a portable fan. In winter, I don't like going out, so I exercise at home. I always put hand warmers in my pocket. On rainy days, I leave home earlier because the traffic is bad. So I always check the weather first.

im2.text: Well, the weather affects my day quite a lot, so the first thing I do in the morning is check the weather app. I look at the temperature, the chance of rain, and the fine dust level. In summer, I wear thin, light clothes, use sunscreen, and carry a small umbrella in my bag, because sudden showers are common. I also try to stay inside during the hottest part of the day. In winter, I dress in layers, like a sweater under a long padded coat, and I never forget my gloves. On days with bad air, I wear a mask and skip my evening jog. So my plans really depend on the weather.
phrases: the first thing I do in the morning is
my plans really depend on the weather

im2.text: I'd say the weather decides a lot of my daily choices. For example, on hot summer days, I take the subway instead of riding my bike to work, because I don't want to arrive sweaty. I also keep a towel and a water bottle in my bag. During the rainy season, I wear sandals and carry a long umbrella. In winter, I change my routine completely. I wake up a little earlier because it takes time to put on all my warm clothes, and I usually drink hot coffee before leaving. On weekends, if the weather is nice, I go hiking, but if it's bad, I just stay home.
phrases: the weather decides a lot of my daily choices

im3.text: Honestly, the weather affects almost everything I do, from what I wear to how I get to work. Every morning, before I even get out of bed, I check the weather and the air quality on my phone. In summer, the biggest challenge is the heat and humidity. I wear breathable clothes, put on sunscreen, and always keep a small umbrella in my bag, because a sunny morning can turn into a heavy shower by lunch. I also try to do errands early in the morning or after sunset. In winter, my routine is the opposite. I dress in layers, wear thermal underwear, and use hand warmers. I also take the bus instead of walking because the wind is really strong. On days with heavy fine dust, I wear a mask and cancel any outdoor exercise.

Well, living in a place with extreme seasons means I have to adjust my routine a lot. In the summer, I start my day earlier than usual. I go jogging around six in the morning, because after nine it's simply too hot to run. I also carry a handheld fan and a water bottle everywhere I go. When the rainy season starts, I keep rain boots at my office and an extra pair of socks in my bag, which has saved me many times. Winter is a different story. I spend less time outside, so I usually work out at a gym near my house. I also use a humidifier at home because the air gets so dry. Basically, I check the forecast every night and plan the next day around it.
phrases: means I have to adjust my routine
which has saved me many times

ih.text: Sure. The weather has a big influence on my daily routine, mostly because the seasons here are so extreme. My habit is to check the forecast every night before bed, so I can decide what to wear and how to get to work the next day. In summer, I try to avoid the heat as much as possible. I leave home a bit earlier to catch a less crowded subway, I always carry a small umbrella and a portable fan, and I wear light, loose clothes that dry quickly. During the rainy season, I keep an extra pair of shoes at my office, because walking in wet sneakers all day is miserable. In winter, I change almost everything. I wear thermal layers under my clothes, put on a long padded coat, and keep hand warmers in my pockets. On days when the fine dust level is high, I wear a mask and cancel any outdoor plans. It may sound like a lot of work, but after so many years, it's become second nature.

Well, I'd say I plan my days around the weather much more than people in other countries probably do. The first thing I do every morning is open my weather app, and I check three things: the temperature, the chance of rain, and the fine dust level. Based on that, I decide pretty much everything. For example, in summer, if it's going to be over thirty degrees, I wear short sleeves, bring a water bottle, and schedule my errands for the evening. If there's a chance of showers, I pack a foldable umbrella, because summer storms here come out of nowhere. In winter, I go into full protection mode. I wear a long padded coat, a scarf, gloves, and sometimes two pairs of socks. I also switch my workouts from outdoor running to an indoor gym. And during spring, when the dust is bad, I keep the windows closed and turn on an air purifier at home. It sounds complicated, but honestly, everyone here does something similar, so it just feels normal.
phrases: Based on that, I decide pretty much everything
I go into full protection mode

al.text: Well, to be honest, the weather probably affects my daily life more than I'd like to admit. Because the seasons here are so extreme, I've developed a kind of routine for each one. Every night before bed, I check the next day's forecast, and in recent years I've also started checking the air quality index, because fine dust has become a real concern, especially in spring. In summer, my main goal is simply to avoid the heat. I wake up early to go for a run before the sun gets too strong, I wear loose cotton or quick-dry clothes, and I always carry a small umbrella, since a clear sky can turn into a downpour within an hour. During the monsoon season, I even keep a spare set of clothes at my office, which sounds extreme, but it has saved me more than once. Winter requires a completely different strategy. I layer up with thermal underwear, a thick sweater, and a long padded coat, and I move my workouts indoors. At home, I run a humidifier because the air gets incredibly dry. I guess what I've learned is that you can't control the weather, but if you prepare well, it doesn't have to control you.
phrases: more than I'd like to admit

al.text: That's a good question, because I think people who live with four strong seasons naturally become pretty good at planning around the weather. For me, it starts the night before. I check the forecast and decide what I'm going to wear, how I'm going to commute, and whether I can do anything outdoors. In the summer, I basically try to outsmart the heat. I schedule meetings and errands for the morning, stay in air-conditioned places in the afternoon, and carry sunscreen, a water bottle, and an umbrella almost everywhere. When the rainy season hits, I switch to waterproof shoes and leave home earlier, because the traffic gets much worse when it pours. Winter is almost the opposite. I don't mind the cold itself, but the dry air and the wind really bother me, so I wear a scarf and a mask, use lip balm constantly, and run a humidifier at home. On weekends, the weather also decides my plans. If it's clear, I go hiking or meet friends at a park, but if the fine dust level is high, I usually cancel and stay in. It might sound like a lot of effort, but for most people here, it's just part of normal life.
phrases: I basically try to outsmart the heat
it's just part of normal life

questions.tip_ko: 날씨 확인 → 계절별로 하는 준비 순서로 말해요. 여름 하나, 겨울 하나만 골라 구체적인 물건(우산, 패딩, 마스크)을 넣으면 쉬워요.

questions.question: Tell me about a time when the weather caused you a problem or surprised you. What happened, and how did you deal with the situation?

il.text: Last summer, it rained a lot. I did not have an umbrella. I got very wet. I went into a store. I bought an umbrella there. Then I went home. It was a bad day.
Two years ago, it snowed a lot in winter. The road was very slippery. The bus did not come. I walked to school. It took one hour. I was late. My feet were very cold.

im1.text: Last July, I went to the beach with my friends. In the morning, the weather was sunny. But in the afternoon, a big storm came suddenly. It rained very hard, and there was thunder. We ran to a café near the beach and waited for two hours. We were wet and cold, but we drank hot chocolate and talked. In the end, it was a funny memory.

Last winter, it snowed a lot one night. The next morning, I had an important exam. The roads were covered in snow, and the buses were very late. I was really worried. So I called a taxi, but there were no taxis. Finally, I walked to the subway station carefully. I arrived just on time. I was so tired, but I passed the exam.

im2.text: One time, the weather really ruined my plans. It was last August, and I was going to Jeju Island for a family vacation. But the day before our flight, a typhoon came, and all the flights were canceled. At first, I was really upset because we had booked the hotel and a rental car. We called the airline and the hotel, and luckily we could change the dates. We went two weeks later instead. The weather was perfect that time, so it worked out well. Since then, I always check the weather forecast before I book a trip.
phrases: At first, I was really upset because

im2.text: I remember a day last winter when the weather surprised me. In the morning, it wasn't very cold, so I just wore a light jacket and went to work. But in the evening, the temperature dropped suddenly, and it started to snow heavily. My bus was stuck in traffic for more than an hour, and I was freezing. I finally got off and walked to the subway. When I got home, I had a fever. I stayed in bed for two days. After that, I learned to always check the evening weather, too.

im3.text: Let me tell you about something that happened during a hiking trip two years ago. My friends and I went to a mountain near Seoul in late October. The forecast said it would be sunny, so we didn't bring rain jackets. But when we were near the top, dark clouds came in quickly, and it started to pour. The trail became really slippery, and we were soaked in just a few minutes. We were a little scared, so we decided to go down slowly and carefully instead of trying to reach the top. Luckily, we found a small shelter halfway down and waited there for about an hour until the rain stopped. When we finally got down, we went to a restaurant and had hot noodle soup. Now we always pack rain jackets, no matter what the forecast says.
phrases: no matter what the forecast says

im3.text: Okay, I had a pretty stressful experience with the weather last summer. I was supposed to give a big presentation at a client's office across town. That morning, there was a heavy monsoon rain, and some roads near my house were flooded. My usual bus route was closed, so I didn't know what to do. I called my manager and explained the situation, and then I looked for another way. In the end, I took two subway lines and walked the last part in the rain. I arrived fifteen minutes late and completely wet. I was so embarrassed, but the client was very understanding because many people were late that day. Since then, I always leave much earlier when heavy rain is in the forecast.
phrases: I didn't know what to do

ih.text: Sure. One experience I'll never forget happened a few winters ago, during a business trip to Gangwon Province. I was supposed to drive back to Seoul on a Friday evening, but that afternoon a huge snowstorm hit the area. Within a couple of hours, the roads were completely covered, and the police closed part of the highway. At first, I panicked a little, because I had an important family event the next morning. I tried to find a bus or a train, but everything was either canceled or fully booked. So I decided to stay one more night. I called a small guesthouse near the station, and luckily they had one room left. The owner was really kind. She made me hot tea and even lent me some dry socks, because my shoes were soaked. The next morning, the snow had stopped, and the mountains looked absolutely beautiful. I took the first train back and made it to the family event just in time. Looking back, it was stressful, but it taught me to always have a backup plan in winter.
phrases: At first, I panicked a little, because
it taught me to always have a backup plan

ih.text: Well, the weather once completely changed a trip I had been planning for months. A couple of years ago, my friends and I booked a camping trip on the east coast in early September. We checked the forecast the week before, and everything looked fine. But on the second night, a typhoon changed direction and started moving toward the coast. Around midnight, the wind got so strong that our tent started shaking, and the rain was coming in from every side. We realized it wasn't safe to stay, so we packed up as fast as we could in the dark and drove to a nearby town. Every motel was full, so we ended up sleeping in the car in a convenience store parking lot. It was cramped and uncomfortable, and nobody really slept. The next morning, we found out that several trees near our campsite had fallen. That's when we realized how lucky we were. Since then, I pay a lot more attention to typhoon news before any trip near the sea.
phrases: We realized it wasn't safe to stay

al.text: Sure, the most memorable weather problem I've had was during my first summer working in Seoul. I lived in a small semi-basement apartment at the time, which was cheap but not ideal, as I soon found out. One evening in late July, there was an incredibly heavy monsoon rain, the kind where you can barely see across the street. I was at work and didn't think much of it until my neighbor called me and said water was coming into the building. I rushed home, and by the time I got there, there were a few centimeters of water on my floor. Honestly, I was shocked and didn't know where to start. My neighbor and I used buckets and towels to get the water out, and we moved my laptop, books, and clothes up onto the bed and the desk. Some things were ruined, like my rug and a few boxes of old letters, but most of my important stuff was fine. The next day, I called my landlord, and he helped me fix the drain and the door seal. A few months later, I moved to an apartment on a higher floor. It was a tough experience, but it made me take heavy rain warnings much more seriously.
phrases: which was cheap but not ideal, as I soon found out
didn't think much of it until
made me take heavy rain warnings much more seriously

al.text: Well, one experience that really stands out happened last winter, and it actually ended up being a good story. I had planned a long weekend in Busan with my sister, and we were supposed to take the train on Friday evening. That afternoon, though, a cold wave hit the whole country, and the temperature dropped to almost minus fifteen degrees in Seoul. On top of that, it started snowing heavily, and there were reports of delays on almost every train line. When we got to the station, the departure board was full of red messages, and our train was delayed by two hours. At first, we were annoyed, because we had a dinner reservation in Busan. But instead of complaining, we decided to make the best of it. We canceled the reservation, found a warm café inside the station, and spent the time planning the rest of our trip and talking about things we hadn't discussed in years. By the time our train finally left, the snow outside the window looked magical. We arrived late, but the city was quiet and covered in white, which we rarely see in Busan. In a strange way, the bad weather made the trip more memorable, and it reminded me that flexibility can turn a problem into an adventure.
phrases: we decided to make the best of it

questions.tip_ko: 날씨 때문에 생긴 일 하나를 정해 언제 → 무슨 문제 → 어떻게 해결 → 배운 점 순서로 말해요. 감정 표현(I was worried)을 한두 번 넣어요.

questions.question: Compare the weather in your country now with the weather when you were a child. Have you noticed any changes? How have these changes affected people's lives?

il.text: When I was a child, winter was very cold. It snowed a lot. Now winter is not so cold. Summer is hotter now. People use air conditioners more. I think the weather changed.
In the past, spring was long. Now spring is very short. Summer comes fast. It is very hot now. Many people stay inside. I miss the old spring. It was nice.

im1.text: When I was young, we had four clear seasons. Spring and fall were long, and winter had a lot of snow. But now, the weather is different. Summer is much hotter and longer, and spring and fall are very short. Also, we have more fine dust these days. Because of this, people use air conditioners and air purifiers a lot. I think life is more uncomfortable now.

I think the weather has changed a lot since I was a kid. In my childhood, it snowed almost every winter, and I made snowmen with my friends. Now it doesn't snow much in my city. Also, the summers are really hot now. In the past, a fan was enough, but now everyone needs an air conditioner. My electricity bill is very high in August. I really miss the old winters.

im2.text: Well, I've definitely noticed some changes in the weather since I was a child. Back then, the four seasons felt clear and balanced. Spring lasted for a few months, and winter was long and snowy. These days, summer seems to start in May and end in late September, and it's much hotter than before. Spring and fall pass so quickly that I barely have time to wear a light jacket. These changes affect people's lives a lot. For example, people use air conditioners almost all summer, and electricity bills go up. Also, heavy rains cause more flooding than before. It worries me a little.
phrases: These changes affect people's lives a lot

im2.text: Compared to my childhood, the weather now feels much more extreme. When I was in elementary school, summer was hot, but it wasn't dangerous. Now, there are heat wave warnings almost every summer, and the news tells old people to stay inside. Winter has changed, too. It's not as snowy as before, but sometimes there are sudden cold waves.
