Another big change is the air. When I was a kid, I never heard about fine dust, but now I check the air quality every day. Because of these changes, people's daily habits have changed. Masks and air purifiers are normal now.

im3.text: Yes, I've noticed quite a few changes, and I think most people in Korea would say the same. When I was a child, the seasons felt very regular. We had a warm spring, a hot but manageable summer, a long and colorful fall, and a snowy winter. These days, summer has become much longer and hotter. Heat waves happen almost every year, and some nights it's so hot that it's hard to sleep. On the other hand, spring and fall have gotten shorter, so it feels like we jump from winter straight to summer. These changes have affected people in many ways. Older people and outdoor workers are at risk during heat waves, and farmers have a harder time because crops are damaged by sudden heavy rain. Personally, I just miss the long, cool autumns I remember from my childhood.
phrases: most people in Korea would say the same
These changes have affected people in many ways

im3.text: Well, when I think back to my childhood, I remember winters with lots of snow and summers that were hot but not unbearable. My friends and I used to play outside until dinner even in August. Now, though, things feel very different. Summers are noticeably hotter, and there are more days when the government sends heat warning messages to everyone's phone. The rainy season is also less predictable. Sometimes it barely rains, and other times it pours so heavily that streets flood. And of course, fine dust has become a daily concern. Because of all this, people's lifestyles have changed. Parents keep their kids indoors on bad air days, and many people now plan their weekends around the weather app. I think we've had to adapt quite a lot.
phrases: when I think back to my childhood
I think we've had to adapt quite a lot

ih.text: Definitely. When I compare the weather now with the weather I remember from my childhood, the differences are pretty clear. Growing up, I remember four balanced seasons. Spring and fall each lasted a couple of months, summer was hot but bearable, and winter almost always brought several days of heavy snow. These days, though, the pattern seems to have changed. Summer starts earlier, ends later, and the heat is much more intense. Some summers, we have weeks where the temperature doesn't drop below twenty-five degrees even at night, which makes it really hard to sleep. Meanwhile, spring and fall have become so short that people joke we only have two seasons now. These changes have had a real impact on daily life. Electricity use goes up sharply in summer, heat-related illnesses have become more common, and outdoor workers have a much harder time. On top of that, sudden heavy rains seem to cause flooding more often. I think it shows that the climate really is changing, and it's not just something we read about in the news.
phrases: people joke we only have two seasons now
it's not just something we read about in the news

ih.text: Well, I've noticed quite a big difference, and I think it's one of the things people my age talk about a lot. When I was little, the seasons came and went almost like clockwork. The cherry blossoms bloomed in April, the rainy season started in late June, and the first snow usually fell in December. Now, everything feels less predictable. The flowers sometimes bloom in March, the rainy season can be short and dry one year and extremely heavy the next, and winters are generally milder, but with sudden, intense cold waves. Summer is the biggest change for me. It's not just hotter, it also lasts much longer. These changes have affected people in several ways. For example, many families now have air conditioners in every room, which wasn't common when I was a kid. Schools sometimes shorten outdoor activities because of heat or poor air quality. And farmers, like some of my relatives, worry a lot about how the weather will affect their crops. Overall, I think people have adapted, but it comes with higher costs and more stress.
phrases: Summer is the biggest change for me
it comes with higher costs and more stress

al.text: Yes, absolutely, and I think it's one of the most noticeable changes in my lifetime. When I was growing up, the four seasons felt balanced and dependable. Spring arrived gently in March, summer was hot but you could still play outside in the evening, autumn lasted long enough to enjoy the changing leaves, and winter reliably brought snow. I have very clear memories of sledding on a small hill near my school every January. Today, the rhythm feels quite different. Summers have become longer and more intense, with heat waves that last for weeks and nights so warm that many people can't sleep without air conditioning. At the same time, spring and autumn seem to shrink every year, and the transition between seasons is much more abrupt. Rainfall has also become less predictable, swinging between dry spells and sudden, intense downpours that cause flooding in low-lying areas. These changes affect people's lives in ways that aren't always obvious. Elderly people and outdoor workers face real health risks in the heat, energy bills rise, and farmers struggle with unpredictable harvests. Even small things, like how often kids can play outside, have changed. So for me, climate change isn't an abstract idea anymore. It's something I can feel in my daily life.
phrases: one of the most noticeable changes in my lifetime
in ways that aren't always obvious

al.text: That's an interesting question, because the weather is something everyone in my generation seems to have strong memories about. When I was a child, I remember the seasons being very distinct and quite predictable. Winters were cold and snowy, and my parents would wake me up early on snow days so we could clear the path in front of our building together. Summers were hot, but they didn't feel dangerous, and the rainy season came and went at roughly the same time each year. Nowadays, I'd say the weather is both more extreme and less predictable. Summers start earlier and stretch well into September, and there are heat warning messages on our phones almost every week in August. Winters are generally milder, yet every so often a sudden cold wave hits and the temperature plunges below minus fifteen. On top of that, fine dust has become a constant topic, which simply wasn't the case when I was young. As a result, people's habits have shifted quite a bit. We check air quality as routinely as the temperature, many households run air purifiers year-round, and outdoor events are often canceled because of heat or rain. I think we've adapted reasonably well, but it does make me wonder what the weather will be like for the next generation.
phrases: which simply wasn't the case when I was young

questions.tip_ko: 어릴 때 날씨 → 요즘 날씨 → 사람들 생활이 어떻게 바뀌었는지 순서로 말해요. 여름 더위나 미세먼지처럼 예를 하나 골라 깊게 말하면 좋아요.

questions.question: These days, many people are worried about extreme weather, such as heat waves and heavy rain. What do people in your country think about this issue, and what do you think should be done about it?

il.text: Many people worry about the hot summer. It is very hot now. Some people get sick. I think it is a big problem. We should save energy. We should use less plastic. I want to help too.
phrases: I think it is a big problem

il.text: People in Korea talk about heavy rain a lot. Some houses get flooded. It is very sad. The government should help these people. I think we should plant more trees. It is important for everyone.

im1.text: These days, many people in Korea are worried about extreme weather. Summers are very hot, and some old people get sick from the heat. Also, heavy rain causes floods in some areas. People talk about it on the news a lot. I think the government should make more shelters with air conditioning. Also, people should save energy and use public transportation. Small actions can help a lot.
phrases: Small actions can help a lot

im1.text: I think most people in my country are worried about extreme weather now. Last summer, there was a heat wave for weeks, and many people couldn't sleep. In some places, heavy rain damaged houses and roads. I think this is a serious problem. First, the government should prepare better for floods. Second, each person should try to save electricity and recycle more. If everyone helps, things can get better.
phrases: I think this is a serious problem

im2.text: Well, extreme weather has become a big issue in Korea recently. Every summer, there are heat wave warnings, and the news reports that elderly people and outdoor workers are getting sick. Heavy rain is also a problem. A few years ago, some areas in Seoul were badly flooded, and people were really shocked. So I think most people now take this issue seriously. In my opinion, the government should improve drainage systems and build more cooling centers for people who don't have air conditioners. At the same time, we should change our own habits, like using less energy and taking public transportation. Both are important.

I think people in my country have different opinions about this issue. Many people are worried because heat waves and heavy rains seem to happen more often than before. They see flooded streets and hot summers and feel that something is changing. But some people think it's just normal weather and don't worry much. Personally, I believe it's a serious problem. I think the most important thing is preparation. For example, cities should check old buildings and roads before the rainy season. Also, companies should let workers rest during the hottest hours. These changes can protect many people.
phrases: have different opinions about this issue

im3.text: Well, I think extreme weather is one of the topics people in Korea talk about the most these days. Every summer, the news is full of reports about heat waves, and a lot of people are worried about their elderly parents or grandparents who live alone. Heavy rain has also become a big concern since some neighborhoods in big cities were badly flooded a few years ago. Most people I know agree that the weather is getting more extreme, but they don't always agree on what to do about it. In my opinion, we need action on two levels. First, the government should invest in better flood prevention and cooling centers. Second, individuals should try to reduce energy use, for example by turning off unused devices and using public transportation. It won't solve everything overnight, but I think it's a good start.
phrases: one of the topics people in Korea talk about the most
we need action on two levels

im3.text: Honestly, I think people in my country are much more aware of extreme weather than they were ten years ago. When I was younger, people just complained about hot days, but now there's real concern. During heat waves, the government sends emergency text messages, and hospitals see more patients with heat-related illnesses. Floods during the rainy season have also caused serious damage in recent years. Because of this, many people feel that extreme weather is no longer a distant problem. Personally, I think the most urgent thing is protecting people who are most at risk, like the elderly, outdoor workers, and people living in semi-basement homes. In the long term, though, we also need to cut down on carbon emissions by using more renewable energy. I think both short-term and long-term efforts are necessary.

ih.text: Sure. In my country, extreme weather has become a serious topic of conversation, especially in the past few years. People used to treat heat waves and heavy rain as just part of summer, but attitudes have changed a lot. After some terrible floods in big cities, where people were trapped in underground parking lots and semi- basement apartments, the public started to see this as a matter of safety, not just discomfort. Still, I don't think we're doing enough. In my opinion, the government needs to focus on two things. First, it should upgrade old drainage systems and make sure vulnerable housing, like semi-basement homes, is safer or replaced over time. Second, it should support outdoor workers, for example by requiring breaks during the hottest hours of the day. At the same time, individuals can't just wait for the government. We can reduce our energy use, recycle properly, and choose public transportation more often. I believe real change happens when both policies and personal habits move in the same direction.
phrases: as a matter of safety, not just discomfort

ih.text: Well, I'd say most people in Korea now see extreme weather as a real problem, although they react to it in different ways. Some people are very worried and try to change their lifestyle, for example by buying fewer things or avoiding single-use plastic. Others feel that one person can't really make a difference, so they just focus on protecting themselves, like buying a better air conditioner. And some older people say the weather has always been unpredictable, so they don't think it's anything new. Personally, I think the evidence is pretty clear that extreme weather is happening more often, and we need to prepare for it seriously. In the short term, cities should improve their warning systems and drainage, and make sure elderly people living alone get checked on during heat waves. In the long term, I think the country has to rely less on fossil fuels and invest more in renewable energy. I also think schools should teach kids about climate issues, so the next generation grows up understanding why it matters. It's a huge problem, but I don't think it's hopeless.
phrases: although they react to it in different ways
the evidence is pretty clear that

al.text: That's a really important issue, and I think public opinion in Korea has shifted quite dramatically over the last decade. Not long ago, heat waves and heavy rain were mostly seen as seasonal inconveniences, something to complain about and then forget. But after several severe floods, including ones where people lost their lives in semi-basement homes, and summers with record-breaking heat, there's a much stronger sense that this is a safety issue and, frankly, a fairness issue. The people who suffer most are usually those with the fewest resources, like elderly people living alone, outdoor laborers, and low-income families in poorly built housing. So when people talk about extreme weather now, it's often connected to questions about who is protected and who isn't. In my opinion, the response has to happen on several levels. Governments should invest seriously in infrastructure, such as modern drainage systems and early warning alerts, and they should gradually replace dangerous housing. Companies should adjust working conditions, for example by allowing breaks during peak heat. And as individuals, we can make choices that reduce emissions, even if they seem small. I don't think there's a single solution, but if everyone takes some responsibility, the impact can be significant.
phrases: public opinion in Korea has shifted quite dramatically
the response has to happen on several levels

al.text: Well, I think extreme weather has gone from being an abstract environmental issue to something people in my country experience personally, and that has changed the conversation. A lot of my friends, for example, now plan their summer around heat warnings, and after the major floods in recent years, many people realized that even a modern city can be surprisingly vulnerable. That said, opinions are still divided on what should be done. Some people believe the government should take the lead with bold policies, like moving faster toward renewable energy and stricter rules for big polluters. Others worry that those policies might hurt the economy or raise electricity prices, so they prefer a slower approach. Personally, I lean toward stronger action, mainly because the cost of doing nothing seems much higher in the long run. That doesn't mean ignoring the economic concerns, though. I think the government could support industries during the transition and help low- income households with energy costs. At the same time, we need practical adaptation measures right now, such as better flood barriers, more urban trees to reduce heat, and community systems to check on vulnerable neighbors. In the end, I believe this is a problem we can still manage, but only if we treat it as urgent rather than optional.
phrases: treat it as urgent rather than optional

questions.tip_ko: 사회 이슈는 사람들 생각 → 내 의견 → 해결 방법 두 가지 순서로 말해요. 정부가 할 일과 개인이 할 일을 하나씩 나누면 정리돼요.
